Tonight is night 0 and is inside every check. A rule set to **Less than** 1 acts on tonight alone. Past nights are never priced and never re-priced, so a night stops being touched the moment your property's date moves past it.

"Last minute" has two rows: **Booking window (days to stay)** **Less than** 3, and **Sellable occupancy (%)** **Less than** 50. It lowers the price by 15%.

- Tomorrow night, 7 of 20 rooms booked (35%): 1 day away and under half full, so the rule fires. Standard drops from $150 to $127.50.
- Tomorrow night, 14 of 20 booked (70%): 1 day away but not under half, so nothing happens.
- Five nights away, 4 of 20 booked (20%): quiet, but 5 is not less than 3, so nothing happens yet. In three days, if it is still quiet, it will.

A booking window rule is a standard rule: it holds its change while both conditions are true and takes it off when either stops. If a late booking lifts tomorrow night to 55%, the 15% cut comes off on the next check.

Read [Price last-minute nights differently](@77) for the click-by-click recipe.

When a booking window rule acts, the change log says how far away the night was and which mark it crossed:

- **Less than** 7: "It had 5 days to go, past the 7-day mark you set."
- **Greater than** 21: "It had 30 days to go, beyond the 21-day mark you set."
- With occupancy on the same rule: "It was 95% full with 17 days to go, past the 90% and 21-day marks you set."

"Past" for a less-than rule means the night has come inside your mark. "Beyond" for a greater-than rule means it is still further out than your mark.

The note under the **Rate Simulator** tab's **Stay date** field says that the date sets the days to arrival. The days are counted from your property's date, not from your computer's, so a property in the United States sees the same number the real run would see, even late in the evening.

Days are counted on your property's calendar. A check that runs at 11 pm on Friday at the property still treats Friday night as night 0. A check that runs at 12:30 am on Saturday treats Saturday night as night 0 and Friday as past.

MAYA's day changes at midnight in your property's time zone, whatever time your night audit runs. MAYA does not read your property system's business date. After midnight, the night before is in the past: MAYA no longer prices it or sends a price for it, and you cannot type a price for it either. Read [Time, weekends, currency and holidays](@106).

Booking speed compares how many bookings a night received in the past day, week or month with how many similar nights in your own history had received at the same point before arrival. A booking with several rooms counts once. Seven levels run from **Stalled** to **Surging**. You pick one, and your rule fires when the night reads that level or beyond.

In the rule builder, choose **Booking speed (recommended)** in the **Metric** dropdown. Three fields appear:

- **Speed**: the level, from **Stalled** to **Surging**. It starts at **Faster Than Normal**.
- **Measured over**: the window MAYA counts in, **Past day**, **Past week** or **Past month**. It starts at **Past week**.
- **Then waits (advanced)**: how long the rule leaves a night alone after acting on it. It starts at **1 week**.

There is no **Compare** dropdown for this condition. The level you pick already says which way the rule looks (see [Picking a level](#picking-a-level)).

A "?" beside **Measured over** opens a panel titled **How booking speed works**. It says in a few lines what this page says in full, with the same example: about 5 bookings expected, 1 reads much slower, 5 or 6 normal, 10 much faster.

Say your rule measures **Past week**, and the night is Friday, November 13, 2026, 40 days away. MAYA counts the bookings made for that Friday in the past 7 days. Then it takes similar Fridays from your own history and counts what each of them received in the 7 days when it, too, was 40 days away. Their average is the night's "expected" count.

It is Sunday, October 4, 2026. Five similar Fridays at The Harbour Inn received 4, 6, 5, 3 and 7 bookings over those 7 days. The highest and the lowest are set aside, and the average of 4, 6 and 5 is 5. So 5 bookings are expected. Here is how the Friday reads, depending on how many bookings it received itself:

| Level, as shown on screen | Reads as | With 5 expected |
|---|---|---|
| **Stalled** | far fewer bookings than similar nights had | 0 |
| **Much Slower Than Normal** | half or fewer | 1 |
| **Slower Than Normal** | clearly fewer | none at this size |
| **Normal** | about the same | 2 to 8 |
| **Faster Than Normal** | clearly more | 9 |
| **Much Faster Than Normal** | twice as many or more | 10 to 17 |
| **Surging** | far more | 18 or more |

Small gaps read as Normal on purpose. With 5 expected, anything from 2 to 8 is inside the ordinary ups and downs, which is why **Slower Than Normal** never shows at this size. The smaller the numbers, the bigger the gap has to be, so a rule stays quiet on small numbers rather than firing on them.

With fewer than five similar nights to compare with, the reading stays within one step of Normal: **Slower Than Normal**, **Normal** or **Faster Than Normal**. That is always the case on a night near a holiday (see [Picking a level](#picking-a-level)).

This is a comparison with your own past. Booking speed does not say how many bookings a night will end up with, and it does not look ahead. It says whether the bookings so far are ahead of or behind what your own similar nights had at the same point.

Expected 5, received 9, with 5 similar nights: Faster Than Normal.

[Booking speed in detail](@35) has the fine print: exactly which bookings count on each property system, how expected is worked out, and the exact lines between the levels for other numbers. [Which past nights your rules compare with](@36) explains how the similar nights are chosen.

You pick one level. The rule fires when the night reads that level or anything beyond it on the same side of Normal.

| You pick | The rule fires when the night reads |
|---|---|
| **Stalled** | Stalled only |
| **Much Slower Than Normal** | Much Slower Than Normal or Stalled |
| **Slower Than Normal** | Slower Than Normal, Much Slower Than Normal or Stalled |
| **Normal** | Normal only |
| **Faster Than Normal** | Faster Than Normal, Much Faster Than Normal or Surging |
| **Much Faster Than Normal** | Much Faster Than Normal or Surging |
| **Surging** | Surging only |

The rules list shows the condition as "booking speed at least Much Faster Than Normal (past week), then waits 2 days". A level below Normal reads "at most". **Normal** shows no word at all.

The five booking speed starter rules show how the levels are meant to work together. The table has their usual sizes. After "Find money I'm leaving on the table" in the five questions, the three raises can be 15%, 30% and 30%, and after "My pricing works" you may get rules copied from your own rates instead. Read [Your starter rules](@27) for what each one says on the review screen and why a property may not have them.

| Starter rule | Speed | Measured over | Then waits | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Slow-date rescue | Much Slower Than Normal | Past month | 1 week | Decrease 15% |
| Slow-date trim | Slower Than Normal, exactly (see below) | Past month | 1 week | Decrease 7% |
| Warm-date bump | Faster Than Normal | Past month | 3 days | Increase 10% |
| Hot-week surge | Much Faster Than Normal | Past week | 2 days | Increase 25% |
| Sudden-spike catcher | Surging | Past day | 1 day | Increase 25% |

Slow-date trim is the one exception to the table above. It fires on exactly **Slower Than Normal**, so that Slow-date rescue handles anything slower. A rule you build yourself cannot do that: picking **Slower Than Normal** in the builder fires on Slower and everything below it.

At a small property, or on nights far out, expected is small and the strongest levels are rarely reached. **Faster Than Normal** and **Slower Than Normal** fire more often, because they include everything beyond them.
Two recipes use the one-step levels: [Cut prices on nights booking slowly](@75) and [Catch a sudden rush](@76).

**Past day**, **Past week** and **Past month** are 1, 7 and 30 booking dates, counting today. A short window reacts to a burst within a day and is noisy on quiet nights. A month smooths the count and reacts later. The starter rules use **Past day** to catch a spike, **Past week** for a surge, and **Past month** for the slow-date rules and the warm-date bump.

The similar nights are always read over the same length of window, at the same distance from arrival, so a long window never compares a month of this night with a week of another.

A rule that cuts counts full days only, ending yesterday: 1, 7 or 30 whole days, on the night and on the nights it is compared with alike. A rule that raises counts today so far too. So a day that has only just begun never makes a night look slow.

After a booking speed rule adjusts a night, it leaves that night alone for the wait you chose: **1 day**, **2 days**, **3 days**, **1 week** or **2 weeks**. A rule saved before the choice existed waits 1 week. The wait is counted per night and per room type, in whole days at your property: a 2-day wait from a change made at any time on Monday is over as Wednesday begins, and the rule reads the night again in the first cycle of that day.

Once a rule has changed a night, it counts only the bookings made since the newest change on that night by itself or by a stronger rule that moves the price the same way, while that change is still on the price. A weaker rule's change never moves where a stronger rule counts from. A stronger rule is one that changes the price by more; at the same change, a rule that watches booking speed is stronger than one that does not, and of two that do, the one set to the faster speed (the slower one, for cuts). [How rules run](@39#which-one-fires-when-several-match) has the full order.

A rule that raises on a fast pace (**Faster Than Normal**, **Much Faster Than Normal** or **Surging**) needs those bookings alone to beat what similar nights get in its whole window. Any other rule compares them with the similar nights over the same days.

So your rules never stack two raises on the same burst of bookings. If cancellations hit a change but bookings made since keep its rule true, the change stays and the count keeps running from when it was made. A price you type starts the count over: after the rule's wait, it counts its whole window again.

**Example: Hot-week surge at The Harbour Inn**

"Hot-week surge" measures **Past week**, fires on **Much Faster Than Normal**, raises 25% and waits 2 days. On Monday, October 12, 2026 it raises Standard for Friday, November 13. On Tuesday it is waiting. On Wednesday, October 14 the wait is over.

[Counting after a rule acts](@35#counting-after-a-rule-acts) covers the rest: the day of the raise itself, changes made by rules you have since switched off, and the exact wording under **Show the numbers**.

**Good to know** · Once three of a rule's changes are on the same night, an amber banner asks you whether to keep adjusting or stop for that night. Until you answer, it keeps going. Read [Rules that keep adjusting](@43).

The change log then says: Cancellations meant "Hot-week surge" was no longer true, so its 25% raise came off. The next sentence gives the numbers.

While the rule is switched off, its changes stay on the price and are not checked for cancellations. Switch it back on with **Apply price adjustments** and the check resumes. With **Skip price adjustments**, its changes on the days the window showed stay unchecked while those days are held, and the rule counts every booking on the books, as with Apply. With the box unticked, cancellations never take its changes off.

A cut on a slow pace never comes off because of how the night books: cancellations only make the night slower. It stays until you type a price for that night, delete the rule, or the night passes. Switching the rule off leaves the cut where it is. Read [When a price change comes off](@40).

A booking speed rule stays quiet on a night when:

- **There is not enough history.** No similar nights could be found and there was nothing nearby to read momentum from, so the condition is never true. A quiet rule leaves nothing in the change log. You see this only when something else changed that night's price while the rule was switched on: **Show the numbers** then reads "There isn't enough booking history yet to say what is usual for this night." and "Booking speed wasn't rated for this night, so rules that watch booking speed left it alone." A property with no bookings in MAYA yet shows nothing at all until the first bookings arrive. Read [Which past nights your rules compare with](@36#not-enough-history).
There is not enough history

- **The price is already at its limit.** A rule that raises does not fire on a night already at the room type's ceiling, and a rule that cuts does not fire on a night already at its floor. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).
The price is already at its limit
- **You chose to stop it on that night.** When the **Rules that keep adjusting** banner asked, you clicked **Stop for this night**. **Let it run again** on the **Rules** tab undoes that.
You chose to stop it on that night

- **The night has no price to start from**, for example a rate of 0 in Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations. Such a night is left unpriced, and no rule acts on it. (On Mews, MAYA does not read your rates, so a 0 there has no effect.)
The night has no price to start from

- **The rule is switched off, or does not change that room type.** Its switch on the **Rules** tab reads **Off**, or the room type is not in its **Change** list. Rules have no dates or days to set, so a rule that is on covers every night in the window.
The rule is switched off, or does not change that room type
- **Every room type the rule measures is unticked as a room.** The rule measures nothing, so it cannot read a pace. Read [Measure one set of room types, change another](@38).
Every room type the rule measures is unticked as a room
- **The rule is waiting.** Its wait on that night and room type is not over.
The rule is waiting

- **Another rule holds the night.** A stronger rule that is waiting, and would be true again on the bookings since its own latest change, keeps a weaker one from firing under it. Read [How rules run](@39).
Another rule holds the night

- **Nothing new to count.** Since the newest change on the night by the rule or a stronger one, too few bookings have come in to read the rule's level. A rule that cuts has nothing to count until a full day has passed since the day of its cut.
Nothing new to count

- **The night is near a holiday and the rule asks for a stronger level.** A holiday night reads at most **Faster Than Normal** or **Slower Than Normal**, so a rule set further out never fires there.

Occupancy rules and booking window rules work from day one. Booking speed needs your history, which is why MAYA imports it as soon as you connect. Read [The history import](@23).

In the Rate Simulator, the **Booking speed** dropdown starts at **Not enough history**, which keeps booking speed rules quiet in the same way. Read [Trying rules out in the Rate Simulator](@44).
The night is near a holiday and the rule asks for a stronger level

**Does a wedding or a group booking count as lots of bookings?** No. A booking with several rooms counts once for booking speed, while all its rooms still count for [sellable occupancy](@32). Rooms booked as separate reservations, for example guests booking from a room block, count as separate bookings. Read [What is counted](@35#what-is-counted).
Does a wedding or a group booking count as lots of bookings?

**Is booking speed a forecast of demand?** No. It describes how a night has booked so far, against your own similar past nights at the same point, and says nothing about where the night will end up. There is no forecast of occupancy or demand anywhere in MAYA. Read [No forecasts](@0#no-forecasts).
Is booking speed a forecast of demand?

**Why did it raise a night that is still empty?** Booking speed does not look at how full the night is. On a quiet night far out, 2 bookings against an expected 0 reads **Much Faster Than Normal**, and a raise rule fires. That is what a far-out rush looks like, for example after a concert is announced months ahead, and it clears the same checks as everything else. If you want raises only on busy nights, add a **Sellable occupancy (%)** row to the same rule, so both must be true.
Why did it raise a night that is still empty?

**Why did it cut a night that is nearly full?** For the same reason. A cut rule reads the pace of recent bookings, not the total. A nearly full night that received nothing this month, against similar nights that received 6, reads slow. Add an occupancy row (**Less than** 70, say) to keep cuts away from full nights.
Why did it cut a night that is nearly full?

**Why does MAYA say Faster Than Normal from only two bookings?** Because similar nights had almost none at the same point, so 2 is a real change. With five or more similar nights behind it, 2 bookings against an expected 0 reads **Much Faster Than Normal**. With fewer than five, the reading stays one step from Normal, at **Faster Than Normal**.
Why does MAYA say Faster Than Normal from only two bookings?

**Why does it say Normal when we got far more bookings than usual?** Usually one of three things. The difference is still small in bookings (with 3 expected, anything from 1 to 5 reads Normal). The bookings came in before this rule or a stronger one last raised the night, and the rule now counts only the ones since. Or the similar nights were as busy at the same point, so this night is keeping pace rather than running ahead. **Show the numbers** in the change log shows the counts.
Why does it say Normal when we got far more bookings than usual?

**Can I see a night's booking speed before a rule acts on it?** Not yet. The calendar does not show it, and the **Rate Simulator** works on a night you make up, so it counts nothing. A real night's reading shows under **Show the numbers** in the change log, under a change on that night, when a booking speed rule was checked there.

To watch for a level while your property is in simulation, add a rule set to the level you are curious about. When a night reads that level or beyond, the rule fires there (unless a stronger rule holds the night), and the change log shows the reading under the change without sending anything. The change log keeps about the last 50 minutes on screen, so look soon after. Delete the rule before you go live. Read [When the reading shows](@35#when-the-reading-shows).
Can I see a night's booking speed before a rule acts on it?

**Can bookings that later cancel move my prices?** For a while, and only inside your floors and ceilings. Every booking still on the books counts for booking speed, whatever channel it came from, so bookings that are made and later cancelled (speculative bookings, test bookings or fake ones) can make a raise rule fire before they cancel. On Mews, enquiries and optional reservations count too. Here is what keeps that in check:

- A cancelled booking leaves the count on the next read, as if it had never been made. It never counts as a negative, so making and cancelling bookings cannot make a night read slower than it would have.
- With the undo box ticked, a raise comes off once cancellations mean its rule is no longer true (read [When a change comes off](#when-a-change-comes-off)). That goes for booking speed, a pickup count **Greater than** and occupancy alike.
Can bookings that later cancel move my prices?

- Once three of a rule's changes are on the same night, the amber banner asks you whether it should keep going.

Read [When a price change comes off](@40) for every case.

Both count what a night gained recently. Booking speed compares the count with your own past nights, so the same three bookings can read as a rush in February and as normal in August. Pickup count compares with a fixed number you type, and counts room nights rather than bookings. That is why the builder labels them **Booking speed (recommended)** and **Pickup count (advanced)**. Read [Pickup count (advanced)](@37) for when a fixed number is the right tool.

**Not yet** · You cannot see a night's booking speed on the calendar or before a rule acts on it. You cannot move the lines between the levels, change the checks that hold small gaps at Normal, or change how many similar nights are used.

This page is the fine print behind booking speed. A booking counts once on each night it covers, dated the day it was made, and only in the room types a rule measures. Expected is the average of what up to eight similar past nights received over the same stretch, with the highest and lowest set aside. Small gaps read as Normal on purpose, so a rule stays quiet on small numbers.

Start with [Booking speed](@34) if you have not read it. It covers what you choose in the builder, the seven levels and which one to pick.

For each night in the window, MAYA counts the bookings made for that night during the stretch your rule measures. Five things set what goes into the count.

**One booking counts once.** A booking is one reservation for one night, however many rooms it holds. A 20-room reservation is 20 booked rooms for [sellable occupancy](@32) and one booking for booking speed.

It counts as one booking on each night it is booked for, and as one booking again whenever one of those nights is later used as a similar night for another date. If a room is added to that reservation a week later, it is still one booking, dated when it was first made, so the added room never reads as a new booking. Rooms booked as separate reservations, for example guests booking from a room block or allotment, count as separate bookings. MAYA does not read room blocks.
One booking counts once

**The date is the booking date.** A booking counts on the day your property system recorded it, not on the day of the stay. For a rule that raises, **Past day** counts bookings dated today, **Past week** today and the six days before it, and **Past month** today and the 29 days before it. "Today" is today on your property's own calendar, so a reading taken at 12:10 am has almost nothing in **Past day** yet. A rule that cuts counts whole days only, ending yesterday: **Past day** is yesterday, **Past week** the seven days up to yesterday. The similar nights are read over the same whole days.
The date is the booking date

**Each night counts its own bookings.** A three-night stay is one booking on each of its three nights, because each night is priced on its own. That is why one booking can turn up in the count for two different nights: it is a booking for both, not two bookings on one.
Each night counts its own bookings

**An extension keeps the booking's date.** When a guest extends a stay, or a booking's dates are changed in your property system, the added nights belong to the same booking, dated when it was first made. They count as booked rooms for sellable occupancy on the next read, but they are usually too old to count in **Past day** or **Past week**. This is the same in Cloudbeds, ThinkReservations and Mews. If the extra nights are booked as a new reservation instead, that is a new booking, dated the day it was made.
An extension keeps the booking's date

**Only the room types the rule measures are counted.** A rule that measures Standard and Deluxe counts bookings in those types and no others. A room type you have unticked as a room is never counted. Read [Measure one set of room types, change another](@38).

When a guest cancels, your property system stops reporting the booking and it leaves the count on the next read. It is not counted as a negative. Every booking counts the same whatever channel it came from: there is no way to count only direct bookings.
Only the room types the rule measures are counted

**ThinkReservations:** ThinkReservations reports each room booking inside a reservation on its own. MAYA groups them back into one booking by the reservation, so a reservation with three rooms is one booking. Every booking counts except cancelled bookings and no-shows. The booking date is the reservation's creation date, on your property's calendar.

**Mews:** A Mews reservation is one room, so each reservation is one booking, including each reservation in a group. Every Mews reservation counts, including enquiries and optional (tentative) and requested ones. Only cancelled reservations are left out. Read [Which bookings count](@14#which-bookings-count). The booking date is the reservation's creation date, on your property's calendar.

A count on its own says little. Three bookings in a week is a rush for a quiet Tuesday in February and a worry for a Saturday in August. So MAYA compares the count with what similar nights in your own history had received by the same point.

Each night is compared with up to eight similar past nights from the last three years: the same weekday (or, near a holiday, the same position around it) and the same time of year. A night near a holiday has 3 similar nights at most, one from each year. [Which past nights your rules compare with](@36) explains how they are chosen and what happens when there are too few.

Expected is the average of those counts. Once there are five or more similar nights, the single highest and the single lowest are dropped before averaging, so one odd night cannot swing the number. The result is kept to two decimals, so expected can be a fraction, such as 0.4 for a quiet night far out. The change log reads "almost none" when it is under 1, and **Show the numbers** reads "almost no bookings". Otherwise both round it to a whole number.

A similar night that has no bookings anywhere in your history is treated as unknown, not as zero, and is left out of the average. A night that has history but nothing in the stretch is a real zero and stays in.

The smaller the numbers, the bigger the gap has to be compared with what is usual before a night reads anything but Normal. With 5 expected you need 9 to read **Faster Than Normal**, nearly double. With 20 expected you need 27, about a third more. The outer levels, **Stalled** and **Surging**, need a bigger gap still. With fewer than five similar nights to compare with, the reading stays within one step of Normal. That is always the case near a holiday.

These checks can only pull a reading towards Normal, never away from it. When one of them kept a reading nearer Normal, **Show the numbers** says so in one of three lines. Each is quoted here only far enough for you to find it:

- "The numbers leaned away from Normal": the gap was too small for this many bookings, so the level stays Normal.

- "Only a few similar nights were found": there were fewer than five similar nights, so the level stays within one step of Normal however strong the numbers look. A reading built from momentum (see [similar nights](@36#momentum-when-nothing-matches)) always counts as one similar night, so it always stays within one step.

**Example: The exact lines, for the curious**

MAYA divides the count by expected, with expected treated as at least 0.5 for the division. At least 1.25 times expected reads Faster Than Normal, at least 2 times Much Faster, at least 3.5 times Surging. The slow side mirrors it: 0.8 times or less is Slower, half or less Much Slower, 1 in 3.5 or less Stalled.

How many bookings a night needs, in the window, to read each level. Computed from the lines and checks above, with five or more similar nights behind the expectation.

| Expected | Stalled | Much Slower | Slower | Normal | Faster | Much Faster | Surging |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (a night far out) | never | never | never | 0 or 1 | never | 2 or 3 | 4 or more |
| 1 | never | never | never | 0 to 2 | never | 3 or 4 | 5 or more |
| 3 | never | 0 | never | 1 to 5 | never | 6 to 10 | 11 or more |
| 5 | 0 | 1 | never | 2 to 8 | 9 | 10 to 17 | 18 or more |
| 10 | 0 to 2 | 3 to 5 | never | 6 to 14 | 15 to 19 | 20 to 34 | 35 or more |
| 20 | 0 to 5 | 6 to 10 | 11 to 13 | 14 to 26 | 27 to 39 | 40 to 69 | 70 or more |

Two things in the table are on purpose. At small expectations some levels can never be reached: with 1 expected, one missing booking is inside the ordinary ups and downs, so the night cannot read slow at all. And with fewer than five similar nights, every "Much" cell and both ends collapse to **Faster Than Normal** or **Slower Than Normal**. Nights near a holiday always read this way, because they never have more than 3 similar nights.

**Example: Where the Friday lands**

Take the Friday from [Booking speed](@34#how-a-night-reads), with 5 expected from five similar Fridays. In the past week it received 9 bookings, 1.8 times the usual, and a gap of 4 is big enough at this size. Five similar nights is enough for the full range. The level is **Faster Than Normal**.

With 10 bookings instead of 9, twice the usual, the level is **Much Faster Than Normal**. With 18, 3.6 times the usual, it reads **Surging**. With 1 booking, a fifth of the usual, the first reading would be Stalled, but a gap of 4 is not enough for the outermost level, so it steps in to **Much Slower Than Normal**.

Once a rule has raised a night, it counts only the bookings made after the newest raise still on that night by itself or by a stronger rule: the rest of the day of that raise, then every day since. A stronger rule is one that changes the price by more, and at the same change the one that watches booking speed, set to the faster speed ([How rules run](@39#which-one-fires-when-several-match) has the full order). A weaker rule's raise never moves where a stronger rule counts from. That includes raises made by booking speed and pickup rules alike, and by a rule you have since switched off, because its raises stay on the price. A raise that came off, for cancellations or because you typed a price, no longer counts as a starting point.

On the day of a raise, a booking counts only if it first reached MAYA from your property system after that raise. So a rush later that day is still counted, and nothing from before the raise is counted twice.

A rule that raises on a fast pace (**Faster Than Normal**, **Much Faster Than Normal** or **Surging**) needs those bookings alone to beat what similar nights get in its whole window. Every other rule reads the similar nights over the same days of their own curves. They had no change that day, so for them the first day counts in full.

When cancellations hit a raise but bookings made since keep its rule true, the raise stays, and every rule keeps counting from when it was made, not from when it was checked. Counting starts again only when a price changes.

The change log says: "Bookings came in much faster than normal in the 3 days since this rule or a stronger one's latest raise still on this night: 12, against the 5 a night like this usually gets in a whole week." Under **Show the numbers** it says: "The newest raise still on this night's price, by the rule behind this reading or a stronger rule, was made on Mon, Oct 12 2026. In the 3 days from that raise on, 12 bookings arrived for it, with 30 days still to go before arrival."

- **Another rule can act on the same day.** If a stronger raise rule fired on the night earlier today, a weaker raise rule can still act on that night today, but only on the bookings that arrived after that raise. The stronger rule holds the night through its wait only while it would be true again on what it counts itself (read [How rules run](@39#which-one-fires-when-several-match)).
Another rule can act on the same day

- **A price you type starts the rule over.** Typing a price on a night takes the rules' changes off it. A booking speed rule then waits its wait, in whole days from the day you typed, and after that it counts its whole window again, including bookings from before your price. Read [Setting a price yourself](@50).
A price you type starts the rule over

You cannot see a night's booking speed on the calendar. The reading appears in the change log, under **Show the numbers**, under a price change on that night when at least one of your booking speed rules was checked there in that run.

- A rule that is switched off, or that you stopped on the night, is not checked.
- A rule that is waiting on every room type it changes that night is checked only when another booking speed or pickup rule is ready to fire on one of them.
- A night whose price did not change shows no reading.

The **Rate Simulator** lets you pick a level for a made-up night, but does not count anything.

A rule that measures every room type ticked as a room reads the whole hotel's history. A rule that measures only some types (Standard alone, say) gets its own counts over the same similar nights, shared with every other rule that measures the same set.

Two things follow. A room type that started selling only last year has no data before its first sale, so it has fewer similar nights and its reading more often stays within one step of Normal. And a small set has a small expected, so small gaps keep the reading at Normal more often. That is by design: a rule on a small set fires less often rather than wrongly.

If a rule on two Suites seems too quiet, widen what it measures: tick **Change prices on different room types**, measure your whole property and change only the Suites.

Each night is compared with up to eight similar past nights from the last three years: the same weekday (or, near a holiday, the same position around it) and the same time of year, skipping closures and any dates you have set aside. A night near a holiday has at most three, one a year. Away from holidays, with too few, MAYA widens the search a step, to other nights of the same kind (weekend or weekday) or a nearby time of year, and says which. With none, it reads booking momentum from nearby nights instead. With nothing at all, booking speed rules stay quiet on that night.

Which past nights count as similar does not depend on the rule, so every rule uses the same ones. What each rule counts on those nights depends on the room types it measures.

You never see the similar nights while a rule is being checked. You see them afterwards, in the change log, and only under a price change: open **Show the numbers** under a change on that night, then **Which nights were compared?**, then **List the nights**. **Show the numbers** is there only when at least one of your booking speed rules was checked on that night in the same run. A rule that is off, or that you stopped on the night, is not checked. A rule that is waiting on every room type it changes that night is checked only when another booking speed or pickup rule is ready to fire on one of them. Read [The numbers behind a change](@48).

For a night that is not near a holiday, MAYA looks for at least 4 similar nights and keeps at most 8. They come from the three years before the night being priced, up to yesterday. A night near a holiday works differently: it is compared with that holiday in each of the three previous years, so it has 3 similar nights at most (read [Holidays](#holidays) below). Some nights are never used, whatever else is true of them:

- nights inside a closed period you confirmed during the review
- nights you have set aside as not a fair comparison
- a window of dates around a yearly event, once your reports from 2 different years agree on it

Read [Closed periods and set-aside dates](#closed-periods-and-set-aside-dates) below.
For a night that is not near a holiday, MAYA looks back through your history, most recent first, in up to three steps. It takes the next step only when the ones before have found fewer than 4 nights.

1. **First, the same weekday in the same season.** MAYA steps back 7 days at a time and keeps the nights inside the same season, never a night near a holiday. The reasons you read are "a Friday", "your Peak Season" (or "your Year-Round"), and "earlier this year", "recently", "about a year earlier", "2 years earlier" or "3 years earlier".
First, the same weekday in the same season

2. **If fewer than 4 are found, the same kind of night in the same season.** Friday and Saturday are weekend nights, and every other night is a weekday night, so a Saturday can stand in for a Friday. The reason reads "a Saturday, similar to a Friday".
If fewer than 4 are found, the same kind of night in the same season

3. **If there are still fewer than 4, the same weekday at a nearby time of year.** Any night on the same weekday within 45 days of the same point in the year counts, whatever the season. The reason reads "a nearby time of year".

When your history is too thin to show seasons, or shows none, the whole year is one season called "Year-Round". The first step then keeps the nearest same-weekday nights, whatever the time of year.

When more than 8 qualify, the best 8 are kept: nights from the first step before the second, the second before the third, and within a step the nearest in time first.
If there are still fewer than 4, the same weekday at a nearby time of year

If the second or third step was needed, the list under **Which nights were compared?** says what was added. After the second step the weekday line names the nights: "Too few other Friday nights matched, so Saturday nights were compared too, since they are also weekend nights. Friday and Saturday nights count as weekend nights, the rest as weekday nights." After the third, the season line says nights within 45 days of the same time of year were added. Either way a line follows: "Fewer than 4 nights matched closely, so the search was widened. Check the nights below and set aside any that were not normal." To check, open **List the nights** and look at the dates. If one of them was not a normal night, set it aside with **Not a fair comparison?** (read [Setting a date aside](@49)).

It is Sunday, October 4, 2026 and the night is Friday, November 13, 2026. The first step goes back a week at a time from the night. Fridays later in October 2026 have not happened yet, so the first candidates are Fri, Oct 2 2026, then Sep 25 and so on, kept only when they fall in the same season as November 13. Then come Fridays from the same season in 2025 and 2024, such as Fri, Nov 14 2025 and Fri, Nov 15 2024. The Friday after Thanksgiving is skipped every year. If fewer than 4 Fridays qualify, the second step adds Saturdays from the same weeks, and the drill-down names them: "Too few other Friday nights matched, so Saturday nights were compared too".

Weekends are Friday and Saturday nights. Sunday is a weekday night. MAYA uses that in two places: in the second step of the search, where a Saturday can stand in for a Friday, and in how seasons are read, which watches how Friday and Saturday nights book against the rest of the week (see [Seasons](#seasons) below). Holidays use a wider weekend of their own: a holiday that falls on a Friday, Saturday or Sunday counts as a weekend holiday (see [Holidays](#holidays) below).

**"Our weekend is Thursday and Friday nights. Can MAYA use a different weekend?"** No. There is no setting for which nights are your weekend. Away from holidays, the first and third steps of the search always compare a night with the same weekday, so your Thursdays are compared with Thursdays and your Saturdays with Saturdays. Only the second step, used when the first finds fewer than 4 nights, groups nights into weekend (Friday and Saturday) and weekday (Sunday to Thursday). There a Thursday can be compared with a Monday, and a Friday with a Saturday. Every date on this page is a date on your property's own calendar. Read [Time, weekends, currency and holidays](@106).

A night inside a holiday's stretch is compared by its position around the holiday, not by its weekday. The Saturday after Thanksgiving is compared with the Saturday after Thanksgiving in each of the last three years, whatever the dates were. Thanksgiving always falls on a Thursday, so there the weekdays line up.

For a holiday on a fixed date, the position around it is the same date every year, so the compared nights usually fall on other weekdays. Saturday, December 26, 2026 (the day after Christmas) is compared with Friday, December 26, 2025, Thursday, December 26, 2024 and Tuesday, December 26, 2023. All three are kept. The fixed-date holidays are New Year's Day, Valentine's Day, St. Patrick's Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Halloween, Veterans Day and Christmas.

A year in which the holiday fell on a similar part of the week scores higher, and the reason reads "similar weekend placement". The parts of the week are a weekend (a holiday on a Friday, Saturday or Sunday), a Monday or Thursday, and midweek (a Tuesday or Wednesday). The score only changes the order of the nights, never which ones are used. When the matching night sits nearer a different holiday that year, it is kept but ranked lower, with the reason "also Father's Day that year".

Under **Which nights were compared?** a line reads "This night is near Thanksgiving, so it is compared with the same days around Thanksgiving in earlier years, not the same date." Above it, the weekday line names the days of the week the compared nights fall on. Around a holiday that moves with the weekday, such as Thanksgiving, they are all the night's own weekday: "Only other Saturday nights were compared, since each night of the week books in its own way." Around a fixed-date holiday they usually differ, and the line lists them: "Around Christmas the day of the week changes from year to year, so the nights compared fall on Tuesday, Thursday and Friday." Under **List the nights**, each night's reasons give the year and the position, for example "Thanksgiving 2025; 2 days after the holiday; similar weekend placement".
