A night inside two stretches belongs to the nearer holiday.

Nights that are not near a holiday are never compared with nights that are. A night near a holiday is compared only with the same holiday in earlier years, with one exception: if none of those past holiday nights has any bookings (for example in your first year), the night is read from momentum, which uses the ordinary nights around it. MAYA does not read weather, event listings or any holiday feed. Its only inputs are your own bookings.

**"My hotel is outside the US. Do Thanksgiving and July 4 still change how my nights are compared? Can I turn them off?"** Yes, they apply to every property, and there is no switch to turn them off. In a year, roughly 64 to 70 nights fall inside one of these stretches. Each of those nights is compared with the same position around the same US holiday in earlier years, and your ordinary nights are never compared with them. When none of those past holiday nights has any bookings, for example in your first year, the holiday night is read from momentum instead, which uses the ordinary nights around it. For a holiday on a fixed date, such as Independence Day (July 4), that means the same dates in earlier years, whatever weekday they fell on. For one that moves, such as Thanksgiving (the fourth Thursday of November), it means the matching days around it.

**Not yet: Your own holidays** · There is no screen to add a holiday, a school break or a local festival, or to switch a US holiday off, and none is read from anywhere. The workaround is to set the dates aside. Open a change on the **Change Log** tab, click **Show the numbers**, then **Which nights were compared?**, then **List the nights**, and click **Not a fair comparison?** under the night. Choose the first reason in the list (the one for a holiday) and the scope **This happens every year around this time**. Once you have reported it from 2 different years, that window is skipped every year. Read [Setting a date aside](@49).

"Season" here means a stretch of your year that books differently from the stretches around it: busier or quieter, with stronger or weaker weekends, or filling earlier or later. Your seasons come straight from your own booking history. They are worked out again each time your rules run, so you never set or maintain them (and cannot edit them).

How seasons are read, in plain terms:

- The input is how many rooms each past night in the last three years sold, and how early it filled. Price is never used, so your own past pricing cannot bend the result.
- MAYA needs booked past nights on at least 120 different days of the year (about four months). With less, the whole year is one season called "Year-Round".

Seasons are named by their level: "Peak Season", "Low Season" and "Shoulder Season" (or "June Shoulder Season" when there are several). When the levels are close and the seasons differ in shape rather than size, they are named by their place in the year instead: "June Season" or "June to August Season".

You will only ever meet a season name inside an explanation, in a line such as "Only nights in the same season of your history were compared: Peak Season (June 10 through August 31)." or "Only nights in the same season of your history were compared: Year-Round (January 1 through December 31)." There is no seasons page and no season setting. Each change log entry keeps the season it used at the time. So an older entry can name a season, or season dates, that no longer match today's. New readings work seasons out again from your current history each time your rules run.

**Not yet: Your own seasons** · You cannot see your seasons in one place, define a season, rename one or move its edges. Seasons are worked out again from your bookings each time your rules run, so a change in how you book changes them with no work from you. If a past stretch is skewing them (a renovation, a one-off event), set those dates aside: any date you set aside, with any scope, stops counting toward your seasons from the next run. Choose **This should also change how our seasons are read (advanced)** only when the same stretch repeats every year. Once reports from 3 different years agree, the whole window around it is left out of your seasons every year.

Sometimes no similar night can be found at all: a room type that has never sold at this time of year, a holiday night whose earlier years have no bookings, a night far outside your history, or a night crowded by set-aside dates. MAYA does not invent a number. It makes one simpler reading, called momentum: how the nights near this one are filling right now, compared with how the same nights were filling a year ago.

In short: if the nearby nights have 6 bookings between them now, against 5 at the same point a year ago, they are filling about 20% faster. If this night itself had 4 bookings at this point a year ago, expected is 4 raised by 20%, about 5.

**Example: The exact steps, for the curious**

- It looks at the 10 nights on either side of the night being priced, keeping only nights that are today or later, not near a holiday, and not set aside. It needs at least 2 of them.

- Each of those nights is paired with the same night 364 days earlier (52 weeks, so the weekday lines up) at the same distance from arrival, when that year-ago night has history and is usable. The paired nights' bookings now, added together, divided by the same nights' bookings a year ago is the momentum ratio, held between 0.15 and 6.
- With no pairs, or when the year-ago nights had no bookings in that stretch, the ratio is 1. In the second case the drill-down still reads "Those nights are filling at about the same pace as a year ago.", because there was nothing a year ago to measure a change against.

Under **Which nights were compared?** the list opens with "Your history has no usable similar nights for this one, so the usual number comes from booking momentum instead." It goes on with lines such as "3 nearby nights could be paired with the same nights last year." and "Those nights are filling about 20% faster than they were a year ago.", and ends with "Momentum is rougher than comparing similar nights, so treat it as a best effort, not a measurement." The year-ago nights behind a momentum read are listed under **List the nights**, and you can set any of them aside like any other comparison.

When there are no similar nights and momentum has fewer than 2 usable neighbouring nights, the reading is "not enough history". A booking speed condition is never true on such a night, so booking speed rules do nothing there. Occupancy and booking window rules are unaffected.

A rule that stays quiet leaves nothing in the change log, because the change log lists price changes. So you only see this reading when something else changed that night's price (another rule, a price you typed, or on Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations a rate change in your property system) while a booking speed rule was switched on. Then **Show the numbers** reads "There isn't enough booking history yet to say what is usual for this night." and "Booking speed wasn't rated for this night, so rules that watch booking speed left it alone."

This happens on a night whose nearby nights are nearly all holiday nights or set-aside dates. It also happens on a property with no bookings in MAYA at all, where no reading is made anywhere, so nothing is shown at all, not even under **Show the numbers**. A night far outside your history, or a room type that started selling recently, still gets a reading: when none of its similar nights has bookings, it is read from booking momentum, capped at Faster or Slower. On a new property it clears on its own once the first bookings arrive.

Booking speed rules also stay quiet when none of the room types a rule measures still counts as a room. Read [Measure one set of room types, change another](@38).

Two kinds of night are never used as a comparison:

- **Closed periods.** Stretches of at least 14 days with no bookings, with normal bookings on both sides, that you confirmed as a closure on the review after the import ("Were you closed ... ?"). Read [Checking what MAYA found](@26).
Closed periods

- **Dates you set aside.** Any night you flagged with **Not a fair comparison?**. It is left out from the next run. Say it happens every year and, once reports from 2 different years agree, a window of 5 days either side is skipped every year. Read [Setting a date aside](@49).

Undoing a set-aside date makes it comparable again on the next run.
Dates you set aside

- "Only other Friday nights were compared, since each night of the week books in its own way." When the second step added other nights of the same kind, it names them instead: "Too few other Friday nights matched, so Saturday nights were compared too, since they are also weekend nights. Friday and Saturday nights count as weekend nights, the rest as weekday nights." With no other Friday at all it says "were compared instead".

- "Fewer than 4 nights matched closely, so the search was widened. Check the nights below and set aside any that were not normal." (only when the second or third step was needed, as described above).
- "Closed periods, and any nights you have set aside as not normal, are never compared."

For a night near a holiday, the season line is replaced by "This night is near Thanksgiving, so it is compared with the same days around Thanksgiving in earlier years, not the same date." The weekday line above it names the days of the week the compared nights fall on, which around a fixed-date holiday such as Christmas usually differ (read [Holidays](#holidays) above).

After the night has already been raised: "Once a rule or a stronger one has raised this night, it counts only the bookings made after the newest of those raises still on the price, the rest of that day included, and reads the nights it is compared with over the same days. A weaker rule's raise, or any cut, doesn't move where it starts." A rule that raises on a fast pace reads instead "and those alone have to beat what the nights it is compared with get in a whole week". A rule that cuts adds "A rule that cuts counts full days only, up to yesterday, on this night and on the nights it is compared with alike." A change made by an occupancy or booking window rule does not count here.

Pickup count is how many room nights (one room for one night) or how much revenue a night gained over 1, 3 or 7 whole days at your property: what is booked now minus what was booked when the window opened. A rule set to Greater than counts today so far and the days before it; one set to Less than counts full days up to yesterday. Cancellations pull it down, so it can be negative. It compares with a fixed number you type. Booking speed is usually the better choice, because it compares with your own similar nights instead.

MAYA records what is booked for a night each time your rules price it: within about five minutes of its bookings changing, and at least once a day. A record stands until the next one, since nothing changed in between. A pickup rule compares two of those records, over the room types the rule measures:
- **now**: what is booked for the night now (for a rule set to **Less than**, when today began, less anything cancelled since)
now

- **when the window opened**: what was booked when the first day of the lookback began at your property

Pickup is now minus then. For pickup, each room on each night counts one: a four-room booking for one night is 4 room nights of pickup. That is different from [booking speed](@34), where the same booking counts once.

**Pickup measures** sets the unit:

- **Room nights (units)**: the number of booked rooms, rounded to a whole number.
- **Revenue (currency)**: the sum of each booked room night's current rate, as your property system reports it, in your property's currency, to the cent. Nothing is converted.

A booking counts the same whatever channel it came from. There is no way to count only direct bookings.
when the window opened

Choose **Pickup count (advanced)** in the **Metric** dropdown. The row shows:

- **Compare**: **Greater than** or **Less than**. Comparisons are strict: **Greater than** 5 means 6 or more room nights, not 5 exactly.
- **Threshold**: the number of room nights, or the amount, starting at 5. It must be 0 or more. Decimals are kept.
- **Lookback window**: **1 day**, **3 days** or **7 days**, starting at **3 days**.
- **Then waits (advanced)**: how long the rule leaves a night alone after acting on it. It starts on **Same as the lookback window**, and also offers **1 day**, **2 days**, **3 days**, **1 week** and **2 weeks**.
- **Pickup measures**: **Room nights (units)** or **Revenue (currency)**, starting at room nights.

A lookback window counts whole days on your property's calendar. It moves on only at your property's midnight, so the passing of time never changes a pickup count in the middle of the day. Only bookings do.

- **A rule set to **Greater than**** counts today so far and the days before it. With **3 days**, that is today, yesterday and the day before: it compares what is booked now with the most recent record taken at or before the moment the day before yesterday began.
A rule set to Greater than

- **A rule set to **Less than**** counts full days only, up to yesterday, because a day that is not over yet would read as slow. With **3 days**, that is the three days before today. A cancellation made today counts against it straight away. A booking made today counts from tomorrow.

Booking speed counts whole days too, in booking dates. Read [Time, weekends, currency and holidays](@106).
A rule set to Less than

When more rooms cancel than book, pickup is below zero. A rule set to **Less than** 0 fires on nights that are losing bookings. A rule set to **Greater than** anything does not fire on them. The threshold itself cannot be negative.

**Example: A pickup rule at The Harbour Inn**

"Quick pickup" is **Pickup count (advanced)** **Greater than** 4 over **3 days**, measuring room nights, and raises Standard, Deluxe and Suite (the builder's default: the types that count as rooms) by 10%.

When the day before yesterday began, the Saturday had 8 rooms booked across Standard, Deluxe and Suite. Now it has 14. Pickup is 6, which is more than 4, so the rule fires and raises Standard, Deluxe and Suite by 10%. It then waits 3 days (the same as its lookback window) before it can act on that night again.

A pickup rule needs a record from when the window opened. When there is none for one of the measured room types, or the most recent one is more than 12 hours older than that moment and your property had no cycle at all in the 12 hours before it, the condition is false and the rule does nothing on that night. An older record on a quiet night is fine: it is still what the night had. This happens:

- **On a newly connected property, or for a new room type.** MAYA starts keeping records the first time your rules run. A 3-day lookback can only be measured once your rules have been running for 3 days.
On a newly connected property, or for a new room type
- **After a long gap in runs**, for example a connection that was down for days. Once your rules run again, the rule measures again after a full lookback.
After a long gap in runs
- **When every room type the rule measures is unticked as a room, or has been switched off in MAYA.** There is nothing to record. Read [Measure one set of room types, change another](@38).
When every room type the rule measures is unticked as a room, or has been switched off in MAYA

- **On the furthest nights of the 396-night window.** A night is first recorded a few minutes after it enters the window at midnight, and needs a record from before its lookback began. A rule set to **Greater than** cannot act on the furthest 1, 3 or 7 nights of the window (its lookback in days), and one set to **Less than** on one night more. Each night becomes measurable as it moves closer.

Records are kept for at least 14 days, whatever lookback your rules use. That is a week more than the longest lookback, 7 days, so a 7-day rule has what it needs once it has run for a week, except on those furthest nights.
On the furthest nights of the 396-night window

A pickup rule works like a booking speed rule. When it fires, its change stays on the price. It then leaves that night and room type alone for its wait: its lookback window unless you chose another in **Then waits (advanced)**. A "?" beside the dropdown says which wait the rule keeps.

When the wait is over, it counts pickup over its lookback window again, but only what came in since the newest change still on the night by itself or by a stronger rule that moves the price the same way: the room nights (or revenue) booked after that change and still booked. A booking from before the change cancelling takes nothing from that count. So a wait shorter than the window never counts the same burst twice, and a 3-day rule with a 1-day wait can raise again the next day only on new pickup.

A rule that has both a pickup row and a booking speed row waits the longer of the two, and each **Then waits (advanced)** dropdown says so beside its shorter options: "(pickup holds it to 3 days)" on the booking speed row, "(booking speed holds it to 1 week)" on the pickup row. Read [How rules run](@39).

**Good to know** · Pickup rules and booking speed rules rank on one list, so a stronger rule's raise covers the weaker ones whichever kind each is: they count only the bookings made after it. A stronger rule changes the price by more, and at the same change a rule that watches booking speed is stronger than one that does not. Read [Counting after a change](@39#counting-after-a-change).

A rule set to **Less than** looks for quiet nights, and a night far in the future with no bookings yet is always quiet. So a cut on low pickup with no **Booking window (days to stay)** row reaches every night of the 396-night window, and each time its wait is over (its lookback window at least, read above) a night that is still quiet gets the cut again, on top of the one before. With a 7-day lookback that is a cut a week on every quiet night: nine cuts in ten weeks on a night nothing has happened to. Cancellations never undo them, since fewer bookings only make the rule truer, and the **Rules that keep adjusting** banner asks you after three changes on a night but the rule keeps adjusting until you answer. Read [Answer the keeps-adjusting banner](@86).

Two things keep this in your sight. The rule builder fills a **Booking window (days to stay)** **Less than** 60 row in the moment your rule takes this shape, with a "?" beside it that says why; change the number or remove the row, and saving never adds it back. And the window that opens when you add the rule or turn it on says how many nights it reaches and that the cut repeats, from the same trial run as its count of days. Read [The rule builder](@31#conditions) and [Turning a rule on](@41#what-the-days-mean). Rules you saved before are left as they are. To cut only the nights that need it, keep a booking window row, or add a **Sellable occupancy (%)** row so both must be true.

With the rule's undo box ticked, as it is on every new rule, a raise made by a **Greater than** pickup rule comes off when cancellations take the pickup it counted to your number or below, and the rule, counted as it would be now with bookings made since, is not true either. A rule set to **Less than** only gets truer as bookings cancel, so cancellations never undo its change. With the box unticked, cancellations never take a change off. While the rule is switched off, its changes stay on the price and are not checked for cancellations. Switch it back on with **Apply price adjustments** and the check resumes. With **Skip price adjustments**, its changes on the days the window showed stay unchecked while those days are held. Read [When a price change comes off](@40).
On screen, pickup always says "bookings". Read it as room nights (or your amount, for a revenue rule).

The **Rules that keep adjusting** banner names the unit: "Pickup over the 3 days it counted came to 6 room nights, against the 4 you set." A revenue rule shows money there. When the count ran from a raise, it reads "Pickup since the raise before its latest one, by it or a stronger rule, came to 6 room nights".

To see exactly what an older rule measures, click **Edit** on it: the rule builder shows every setting as saved. Change what you want and click **Save changes**, or click **Cancel editing** to leave it as it is.

Both look at what a night gained recently. The difference is what the count is compared with. Pickup's fixed number is right for some nights and wrong for others: 5 room nights in 3 days is a rush for a quiet Tuesday and nothing special for a Saturday in peak season.

|  | Pickup count | Booking speed |
|---|---|---|
| Compares with | a fixed number you type | what similar past nights had received by the same point |
| Counts | room nights, or revenue | bookings (a booking with several rooms counts once) |
| Window | 1, 3 or 7 whole days at your property | past day, week or month, in booking dates |
| Needs history | no, only records from the window start | yes, similar past nights |
| Same count in February and August | reads the same | reads differently, against each season's own pace |

Pickup suits a fixed line you already trust, a property with no history yet, or a rule that should watch revenue. Booking speed suits everything else, which is why the rule builder labels it **Booking speed (recommended)**.

When you click **Get suggestions from my data** on the **Rules** tab, MAYA may suggest removing a pickup rule that one of your booking speed rules already covers (it measures and changes at least the room types your pickup rule does, on at least the same days and dates). The suggestion reads: "Your booking speed rules already cover the same nights by comparing with your own similar past nights. Keeping both would stack two price changes on the same bookings.", after a first line saying the pickup rule reacts to a fixed booking count. You choose **Remove it**, **Turn it off, keep it** or **Leave it running**. Nothing changes unless you accept. Read [Getting suggestions later](@29).

The **Rate Simulator** has a **Picked up** box per room type, in rooms. A revenue rule is tested by valuing those rooms at the base price you typed for that room type.

**Not yet** · The rule card does not show whether a pickup rule measures room nights or revenue. Put it in the rule's name when you build it, for example Pickup 3 days revenue.

Tick **Change prices on different room types** and the rule watches one list of room types (**Measure**) and prices another (**Change**). Only room types that count as rooms can be measured. Anything can be changed. Unticked, one list does both.

In the rule builder, the room types field starts as one list, **Apply to room types**, with every type that counts as a room ticked. Under it is a checkbox, **Change prices on different room types**, with a "?" beside it that opens a panel titled **Measure and change**:

- "You watch occupancy, pickup and booking speed on the Measure room types."
- "When the rule fires, you change prices on the Change room types."
- "Unticked, one list does both."

Tick it and the field splits in two:

- **Measure**: the room types the rule reads its numbers from. Only room types that count as rooms are offered here, because occupancy and booking speed are only ever counted over rooms.
- **Change**: the room types whose prices the rule changes. Every active room type is offered, including ones tagged "not a room".

- A room type that does not count as a room is never measured, on its own or alongside rooms. If you select only the Meeting Room, the rule still prices it but measures nothing. Any sellable occupancy, booking speed or pickup count condition on it can never be true, so the rule never fires. Only a booking window condition, which reads no room types, still works.
- To price a type on its own bookings, tick it as a room on the **PMS** tab (which also counts it in your occupancy and in the rooms you are billed for), then build the rule. There is no other way to measure it.
- With the checkbox unticked and nothing selected: "Select at least one room type."
- With the checkbox ticked and **Measure** empty: "Pick at least one room type to measure."
- With the checkbox ticked and **Change** empty: "Pick at least one room type to change."

- **Sellable occupancy** is rooms booked divided by rooms you can sell, over the measured types only. A rule measuring Standard reads Standard's occupancy, which can differ from the day card's whole-hotel figure. Read [Sellable occupancy](@32).
Sellable occupancy

- **Booking speed** counts bookings in the measured types only, on the night being priced and on every similar past night. A measured set smaller than the whole hotel gets its own counts, shared by every rule that measures the same set. Read [Booking speed on part of the hotel](@35#booking-speed-on-part-of-the-hotel).
Booking speed
- **Pickup count** adds up room nights (or revenue) gained over the measured types. Read [Pickup count (advanced)](@37).
Pickup count

- **Booking window** reads no room types. It is the same number of days for every type.

For occupancy and pickup, one reading serves every room type the rule changes. A booking speed rule can read each changed room type separately, because each one counts from the newest change still on it by that rule or a stronger one. Either way, the rule fires and waits separately for each changed room type, so Suite and Deluxe can each be on a different step of the same rule. Read [How rules run](@39).
Booking window

On the **Rules** tab, the **Room Types** column normally lists the types the rule changes. When the rule measures something different, it reads "Watches Standard, Deluxe · Changes Suite". Only measured types that count as rooms are named there, because those are all the rule measures.

The **Rate Simulator** shows the same thing beside the rule under **Rules in play**.

When a rule measures different room types from the ones it changes, its change log sentences say so:

- "Standard and Deluxe were 92% full, past the 90% mark you set."
- "Standard and Deluxe bookings came in faster than normal this past week: 9, against the 5 a night like this usually has by now."

**Example: Suites that follow your standard rooms**

The Harbour Inn has 12 Standard rooms, 6 Deluxe and 2 Suites. Two Suites are too few to read on their own, so Priya builds "Suites follow": **Sellable occupancy (%)** **Greater than** 80, **Increase the rate** 10%, checkbox ticked, **Measure** Standard and Deluxe, **Change** Suite.

On a Friday with 11 of 12 Standard and 5 of 6 Deluxe booked, the measured occupancy is 16 of 18, which is 89%. The rule fires and raises the Suite from $300 to $330. The Suites' own bookings play no part.

"Busy nights, Deluxe only" measures Standard, Deluxe and Suite and changes only Deluxe. Whole-property occupancy above 80% raises Deluxe alone. Standard and Suite keep their prices.

**Example: A meeting room priced from the rooms**

"Busy nights, Meeting Room" measures Standard, Deluxe and Suite and changes only the Meeting Room. The Meeting Room's price follows how full the hotel is, and its own bookings never count towards occupancy.

A rule reads its numbers only from room types that count as rooms. What happens with the rest:

- **A rule saved with a mixed list** (Standard and the Meeting Room, say, before you unticked the Meeting Room on the **PMS** tab) keeps pricing every type in its **Change** list, but the Meeting Room drops out of what it measures. The change log tells you: "That 95% leaves out Meeting Room."
A rule saved with a mixed list

- **A rule whose measured types have all been unticked** measures nothing. Any sellable occupancy, booking speed or pickup count condition on it can never be true, so it stops firing. It stays **On** on the **Rules** tab, with no warning. A standard rule's change comes off. A booking speed or pickup rule's earlier changes stay where they are.
A rule whose measured types have all been unticked

- **A rule whose measured types have all been switched off in MAYA** (during the review) stops running. Any price change it had already made on the types it changes stays in place, as if the rule were switched off. To clear it, delete the rule or type a price for those nights. Editing the rule to measure active room types, with **Apply price adjustments**, judges those changes against the edited rule. Removing a room type in your property system does not switch it off in MAYA, so the rule keeps measuring it. [Room types and rooms out of service](@52) says what happens to a removed room type in each system, and [Contact support](@111#your-property-system) lists what you can ask us to change.
A rule whose measured types have all been switched off in MAYA

**Good to know** · Whether a room type counts as a room is set on the **PMS** tab with the **Counts as a room** checkbox. Unticking a type takes it out of occupancy, booking speed, the revenue per room behind the calendar colours and the room count you are billed for. It can still be priced. Read [Room types and rooms out of service](@52).

**Not yet** · A rule cannot measure a room type that does not count as a room, on its own or alongside rooms. To price a meeting room or a court on its own bookings, tick it as a room on the **PMS** tab. To price it from how full the hotel is, **Measure** your rooms and **Change** it. A rule also cannot measure one set of room types for occupancy and a different set for booking speed. Two rules, one for each, act separately, and their changes stack.

About every five minutes MAYA reads your bookings and checks every rule again on each night whose bookings changed, for each room type. Once a day, just after midnight at your property, it checks every rule on every night from today to 395 days out. Standard rules (occupancy, booking window) switch on while their condition holds and off when it stops. Booking speed and pickup rules fire, keep their change on the price, wait, and can fire again on the bookings made since. Percent changes compound, fixed amounts add, and the result stays between the floor and ceiling.

A cycle is one run of MAYA for your property. It comes round about every five minutes. Each cycle:

1. reads your bookings from your property system
2. refreshes your own rates when they are due (Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations)
3. runs every rule, for every room type, on the nights that need it: every night whose bookings changed since the last cycle, every night a change of yours reaches, and, in the first cycles after midnight at your property, every night in the window, nearest nights first
4. sends the prices that changed, if your property is live (Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations)

Waits and lookback windows count whole days at your property, so time passing never changes a price during the day: a night nothing happened to keeps its price until the next day's pass.

On Mews, a cycle reads your bookings and runs your rules, and that is all. Your own rates are not read and nothing is sent, live or not. Read [Nothing is sent to Mews](@14#nothing-is-sent-to-mews).

Typing a price on the calendar runs the rules again on those nights at once, without waiting for the next cycle. If a cycle cannot read your bookings, it prices nothing and sends nothing, and the next cycle tries again.

Your rules price tonight and the next 395 nights: 396 nights in all, about 13 months. "Tonight" is the calendar date at your property, in your property's time zone, at the moment the cycle runs.

- Tonight is night 0 and is always priced.
- A night 395 days away is the last one in the window. A night 396 or more days away is not in it, which is why a rule can fire 395 days out and not 397. The night comes into the window at your property's midnight and is priced in that day's pass.
- Past nights are never priced or re-priced. Once your property's date moves past a night, every change on it is left as it was.
- A price you type further ahead (up to 399 days) is saved now. Your rules price it, and it is sent, once the night enters the window.

The **How rules behave** panel on the **Rules** tab shows three short animations: a booking speed rule that raises and waits, an occupancy rule with no wait, and a stronger rule covering a weaker one. A checkbox at the top, "Try the box", plays them with the undo box ticked or unticked. Under them the panel says the box works the same way on every rule, raise or cut, and that turning a rule off keeps its changes as they are.

|  | Standard rule | Booking speed or pickup rule |
|---|---|---|
| Conditions | Only sellable occupancy and booking window | Has a booking speed or pickup count row (with or without the others) |
| How it acts | Switches on when its condition starts to hold, keeps one change on the price while it holds, switches off when it stops | Fires, and the change stays on the price when the condition stops holding |
| Same night twice | Never. One change while the condition holds | Yes. After its wait, if the bookings made since keep it true, it fires again and the changes stack |
| When the change comes off | When its condition stops holding. With its undo box unticked, falling occupancy never takes it off | With its undo box ticked, when cancellations mean the rule is no longer true. Either way, when you set a price, the night passes or you delete the rule |

Read [When a price change comes off](@40) for the undo box and every other way a change comes off.

Every night and room type has a base price, and rules are applied on top of it. MAYA takes the first of these that exists:

1. a price a person set for that night: typed in MAYA, or changed in your property system on a night MAYA had already sent to
2. your own rate for the night, read from your property system

Nothing else. A night with neither is not priced: not the rate a guest paid for it, and not a base saved on an earlier run. A booking taken at one of MAYA's own prices would otherwise come back as the next starting point and climb with every booking. On Mews, your own rates are not read and a rate changed in Mews is never read back, so the base is a price you typed in MAYA, and a Mews night without one is unpriced. Read [Where a night's starting price comes from](@14#where-a-nights-starting-price-comes-from).

If your system shows the night's rate as 0 (a closed night, for example), or has no rate for the night at all, and you have not typed a price, MAYA leaves the night unpriced. No booking speed or pickup rule fires on it, nothing is sent and the calendar shows a dash for its price, with "No rate in Cloudbeds for this night yet" (or your system's name) when the rate is missing. MAYA reads your rates as far ahead as your system returns them and keeps that night on record; a night past it counts as having no rate until a read returns it. This applies on Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations, where MAYA reads your rates.

Standard rules still switch on and off on that night as their condition starts and stops holding, and each switch-on counts in **Fired**. So once the night has a rate, any standard rule already on there applies straight away, and the change log shows it from then.

For each night and room type:

- **Activate.** The conditions hold and the rule was not active there. The change goes on the price. This counts as one fire in the **Fired** column.
Activate
- **Hold.** The conditions still hold. Nothing changes, and the rule does not fire again.
Hold

- **Deactivate.** The conditions stop holding. The change comes off and the price goes back.

So a cancellation that drops a night from 82% to 78% takes a "Greater than 80" raise off on the next cycle. A late booking that lifts it back above 80 puts it on again, and that counts as another fire. With the rule's undo box unticked, a **Greater than** occupancy condition counts as met for as long as the change is on, so falling occupancy never takes the raise off. A booking window condition still runs out as the night gets closer.
Deactivate
- **Fire.** The conditions hold, the rule is not waiting on that night and room type, and it wins the competition (below). The change goes on the price. One fire.
Fire

- **Wait.** The rule leaves that night and room type alone for its **Then waits (advanced)** setting, 1 day to 2 weeks. A booking speed row starts at 1 week. A pickup count row starts on **Same as the lookback window**. A rule with both waits the longer of the two. The wait counts whole days at your property: a 2-day wait from a fire at any time on Monday is over as Wednesday begins, and the rule reads the night again in the first cycle of that day.
Wait

- **Read again.** When the wait is over, the rule reads the night again, counting only the bookings made since the newest change on that night by itself or by a stronger rule that moves the price the same way, while that change is still on the price. Changes made by rules you have switched off count too, because they stay on the price. If those bookings keep the rule true, it fires again and the change stacks on the earlier one. Read [Counting after a change](#counting-after-a-change).
Read again

- **Tell you at three.** Once three of a rule's changes are on the same night, an amber banner asks you whether to keep going. Read [Rules that keep adjusting](@43).

The change log shows a repeat as "Then "Hot-week surge" raised it another 25%, from $250.00 to $312.50."

A 2-day wait after a raise on Monday afternoon: the rule reads the night again as Wednesday begins, and through that day, and counts only the bookings made since the raise, Monday afternoon through Wednesday. A rule that raises on a fast pace needs those alone to beat what similar nights get in a whole week.

**Example: A 2-day wait after a Monday fire**

The starter rule "Hot-week surge" is **Much Faster Than Normal** or faster over **Past week**, waits **2 days**, raises 25%. It fires on the Saturday's price on Monday afternoon.
Tell you at three

Tuesday: waiting. Wednesday, just after midnight: the wait is over. The rule now counts the Saturday's bookings that came in after Monday's raise, from Monday afternoon on, and through Wednesday as they come. Because it raises on a fast pace, those bookings alone have to read Much Faster Than Normal or faster against what similar Saturdays get in a whole week. It never re-counts the bookings that made it fire on Monday.

If Monday's burst was the whole story, the bookings since the raise read Normal and the price holds at one raise. If bookings keep coming, it raises again on Wednesday, waits until Friday, and so on. At three raises on that night, MAYA asks you.

**"My rule's wait is over and the night still reads faster, so why did it not act again?"** Because the whole-window reading you see in an older log entry includes the bookings the rule already acted on. After a change, the rule only counts what arrived since. If those bookings alone do not keep it true, it does nothing. That is by design: your rules never stack two raises on the same bookings.
"My rule's wait is over and the night still reads faster, so why did it not act again?"

Once a rule has changed a night, it counts only the bookings made since the newest change on that night by itself or by a stronger rule that moves the price the same way. A weaker rule's change never moves where a stronger rule counts from, and raises and cuts never move each other's count. A change that has come off no longer counts as a starting point. A change still on the price from before its rule was edited (one **Skip price adjustments** holds, or one of a rule edited while it was off) is judged as the rule was when it made it: an edit that lowers the rule's amount or changes its speed does not change which rules that change covers.

- **A rule that raises** counts from the raise itself: on the day of the raise, only the bookings that reached MAYA after it, then every day since. A rule that raises on a fast pace (**Faster Than Normal**, **Much Faster Than Normal** or **Surging**) needs those bookings alone to beat what similar nights get in its whole window. Any other booking speed rule compares them with similar nights over the same days.
A rule that raises

- **A rule that cuts** counts full days only, up to yesterday, on the night and on the nights it is compared with. After a cut it counts the full days after the day of the cut, so it has nothing to judge until one of those has passed.
A rule that cuts

- **A pickup rule** counts, inside its lookback window, only the room nights (or revenue) booked after the change and still booked. One set to **Less than** counts full days only, up to yesterday, so its last change counted the days before its own. It judges again once a whole lookback window of full days, starting with the day of that change, has passed, because a short stretch always looks slow.
A pickup rule

- **When cancellations hit a change** and bookings made since keep its rule true, the change stays, and every rule keeps counting from when it was made. Counting starts again only when a price changes.
When cancellations hit a change
- **A price you type** starts every rule over: each waits its wait from your price, then reads its whole window again.
A price you type

- **After you skip.** **Skip price adjustments** moves no rule's count. A rule you add, switch on or edit counts as it would with **Apply price adjustments**: a new rule counts every booking in its window, the ones made before you added it included, and an edited booking speed or pickup rule reads its whole window again. On the days the window showed, the rule makes no change until it stops being true there and then becomes true again, and it is judged there on that same count. Skipping starts no wait. Read [Turning a rule on, Apply or Skip](@41#skip-price-adjustments).
After you skip

On Tuesday 3 more book, and on Wednesday one of Monday's guests cancels. "Ten" still has 12 in its week, so its raise stays, and both rules keep counting from Monday's raise. On Thursday 2 more book: 5 since the raise, so "Five" raises 10% on top: $132. "Ten" still counts from its own raise, 5 so far, because a weaker rule's raise never restarts a stronger rule's count.

At most one booking speed or pickup rule fires on a given night and room type in one cycle. When two or more are true and not waiting, the stronger one fires. The first step where they differ settles it:

1. The bigger change to the price, in money on that night's price, comes first (10% of $200 is $20, which beats $15).
2. At the same change, a rule with a booking speed condition comes before one without, and of two with one, the faster speed comes first for a raise (the slower speed for a cut).
3. Next, the pickup count that is harder to meet comes first (**Greater than** 6 before **Greater than** 4).
4. Next, starter rules come before rules you build, in this order: Sudden-spike catcher, Hot-week surge, Warm-date bump, Slow-date rescue, Slow-date trim. Every rule you build ranks the same at this step.
5. Next, the rule with more conditions comes first.

That order is what "stronger" means everywhere in MAYA, including where a rule counts from. The "?" panels in the rule builder give the short version: a stronger rule changes the price by more, and at the same change, a rule that watches booking speed is stronger, set to the faster speed (the slower one, for cuts).

A stronger rule that is still waiting can hold the night. It holds a weaker rule that moves the price the same way only when it would be true again on what it counts itself, the bookings since its own latest change. Then nothing fires on that night this cycle. It holds a rule that moves the price the other way while its whole window still matches. A stronger rule can always fire while a weaker one waits.

Hot-week surge then waits 2 days, and both rules count only the bookings made after its raise. If 9 more arrive by Tuesday, that reads faster than normal against the usual 5 for a week, so "Busy week" raises 10% on top. If 10 or more arrive, Hot-week surge would be true again on its own count, so it holds the night and "Busy week" cannot fire under it.

Before ranking, a rule is dropped for that night when it could not move the price: a raise on a night already at its ceiling, a cut already at its floor, a percent on a price of 0, or any raise on a night you set to 0.

Standard rules do not compete. Every standard rule whose condition holds applies.

For each night and room type, MAYA starts from the base price and applies:

1. every active standard rule change, in a fixed order that is not the order you made them (this only matters when a percent rule and a fixed-amount rule both hold on the same night)
2. every open booking speed and pickup fire, in the order they were made
3. the floor and ceiling

Percent changes multiply: $200 raised 10% is $220, and 25% on top of that is $275, not $270. Fixed amounts add: $200 plus $25 is $225. The result is rounded to cents, and that is the only rounding there is. There is no setting to round to whole numbers or to make prices end in 9. For a price such as $199, type it yourself. Rules that fire later still stack on it and round to the cent. If it would go above the room type's ceiling, the ceiling is published. If it would go below the floor, the floor is.

You can only type a price inside the floor and ceiling, or 0 for a comp night. If a limit changes later, a price you already typed stays as you typed it. Rules on top of it are held between the limits, stretched to include your price. Say Standard's floor was $60 when you typed $70, and you later raised the floor to $80. Your $70 stays. A cut rule can take it no lower than $70, and a raise can go up to the $300 ceiling.

$200, up 10% to $220, then up 25% to $275. The $300 ceiling is not reached, so $275 is published.

Now a festival night, with Standard's rate at $290 and its ceiling at $300: "Busy nights" asks for $319. The change log adds "That would have gone past your $300.00 ceiling for Standard, so it stopped there." and $300 is published. "Hot-week surge" does not fire on Standard at all, because a raise cannot fire on a night already at its ceiling. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).

Your rules check a night within about five minutes of its bookings changing, and every night in the window once a day, and a night's price changes only when something changes it, and it is sent to your property system only when it changes (Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations, once you are live). On a quiet property, hours can pass with nothing sent. Guests do not see a price bouncing every five minutes.

What can move a night's price, and how often:

- **A standard rule** changes it once when its condition starts to hold and once when it stops. A booking window rule starts to hold as the night gets closer. An occupancy rule on a night that hovers around its line can switch on and off as bookings arrive and cancel.
A standard rule

- **A booking speed or pickup rule** changes it at most once per wait. At most one of these rules fires on a night and room type each cycle. With its undo box ticked, cancellations can also take one of its changes off.
A booking speed or pickup rule
- **Three changes** by the same rule on the same night bring the **Rules that keep adjusting** banner, which asks whether it should keep going.
Three changes

- **You**, when you type a price, and **your own rate**, when it changes in your property system.

So a night can still change more than once in a day when bookings come and go, but never only because time passed: a wait or a lookback window moves on only at your property's midnight.
You

Everything above happens separately for each room type the rule changes. Waits run per night and room type. Floors and ceilings are per room type. So a rule can fire on Deluxe and not on Standard on the same night: Standard may still be waiting, sitting at its ceiling, or measured differently. The **Fired** column counts every time the rule acted, once per night and room type each time.

Turning a rule off freezes what it has done: its changes stay on the price, cancellations do not take them off, and nothing new happens. An edit saved while it is off changes nothing either, until you switch it on. Deleting a rule undoes everything it did from the next cycle. Read [Turning a rule off, deleting it, or changing it](@42).

The **Change Log** tab lists every pricing run that changed a price, with the chain of rules and running prices for each room type and night, so stacking is visible. Under a booking speed change, **Show the numbers** opens the counts behind it. Read [The change log](@47) and [The numbers behind a change](@48).

**Careful** · In simulation everything above runs and is written to the change log, but nothing is sent. After you go live on Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations, changed prices go to your property system every cycle. Nothing is sent to Mews. Read [Simulation mode](@54).

A standard rule's change comes off when its condition stops holding. A booking speed or pickup rule's change comes off when cancellations mean the rule is no longer true, as long as its undo box is ticked, which it is on every new rule. A cut on a slow pace never comes off because guests cancel. Your typed price takes earlier changes off that night. An edit you apply judges the rule's changes against the edited rule, and one you save with Skip leaves them on the days the window showed until the rule stops being true there and then becomes true again. Deleting a rule undoes everything it did. Turning a rule off undoes nothing.

Every rule has one box, **Undo the change if cancellations mean this rule is no longer true**, under **Rate adjustment** in the rule builder. It starts ticked on every new rule, and starter rules and accepted suggestions are ticked too. The rules list does not show it. To change it on a saved rule, click **Edit** on the rule, tick or untick it and click **Save changes**. On a rule that is on, the window with the calendar opens first: ticking can take off a change whose rule is no longer true, and unticking can keep one that would have come off. The new box applies from the next cycle, and the rule keeps its changes and its count. Read [Changing a rule](@42#changing-a-rule). The "?" beside the box sums up this page.

- **Ticked.** When a booking that a change counted cancels, MAYA checks the rule again. If the rule is no longer true for that night, the change comes off. If bookings made since keep it true, the change stays.
Ticked

- **Unticked.** Cancellations never take the change off.

The box works the same way for a raise or a cut and for every kind of condition. Cancellations can only make a rule untrue through a **Greater than** occupancy or pickup line, or a booking speed the rule needs at least. A booking window, anything **Less than** and a slow pace only get truer as guests cancel, so a cut made because a night was booking slowly stays when cancellations slow it down further.

Once a change has come off, its rule can change the night again when it is true again and its wait is over. The wait still runs from the change that came off, so a night on the edge does not go up and down every cycle. A standard rule has no wait, so it goes back on as soon as it holds again.
Unticked

A standard rule (only **Sellable occupancy (%)** and **Booking window (days to stay)** rows) holds one change on a night and room type while its condition holds, and takes it off on the first cycle where it does not. With the undo box ticked, that includes a night that drops under its occupancy line because guests cancelled.

**Example: A cancellation at The Harbour Inn**

"Busy nights" raises 10% when a night is more than 80% full. Friday is 17 of 20 booked (85%): Standard is $165. Two guests cancel, so Friday drops to 15 of 20 (75%). On the next cycle, about five minutes later, the raise comes off and Standard goes back to $150. If a new booking lifts Friday over 80% again, the raise goes back on.

With the box unticked, a **Greater than** occupancy condition counts as met for as long as the change is on, so falling occupancy never takes the raise off. The rest of the rule is read as the night is now: a booking window condition still runs out as the night gets closer, and a **Less than** occupancy rule still switches off when bookings lift the night over its line. On a day that **Skip price adjustments** holds, the box keeps nothing, because the rule made no change there: a night that falls under the line ends the hold, and the next time it is over the line the rule adjusts (read [Turning a rule on, Apply or Skip](@41#skip-price-adjustments)).

A booking speed or pickup rule's change stays on the price after the rule fires. With the undo box ticked, cancellations take it off only when they make the rule no longer true. The check starts once a room that was booked for the night when the change was made has cancelled. It recounts what the change counted, not the night as it is now:

| The rule's condition | What the check looks at |
|---|---|
| Booking speed | The bookings the change counted that are still booked, against what a night like it usually got over those days, as read when the change was made. The rule's own level is the bar |
| Pickup count **Greater than** | The pickup the change counted, less the bookings from that stretch that have cancelled since |
| Sellable occupancy **Greater than** | The night's sellable occupancy now |

If the change's own count falls short, MAYA reads the rule once more the way it would count with the change off, bookings made since included. If that keeps the rule true, the change stays and every rule keeps counting from when it was made. Only when both fall short does the change come off.

Each stacked change is checked on its own numbers. A change is never checked in the cycle that made it, never while its rule is switched off, never once the rule measures a different set of room types from the one it measured when it fired, and never when it was already on the price when the rule was last switched on or saved with **Skip price adjustments**.

The change log then says: Cancellations meant "Hot-week surge" was no longer true, so its 25% raise came off. Of the 12 bookings it counted, 9 are still booked, where nights like it usually get about 5, and the rule needs a booking speed of at least much faster than normal. When nothing else is left on the night, the entry ends with the move back, such as "That took this night from $250.00 to $200.00."

A cut rule whose conditions are a slow pace, a pickup count **Less than** or a booking window never comes off because of how the night books. Guests cancelling only make it truer, and new bookings are what the cut was for: a cut that switched off the moment a booking arrived would undo the thing that brought the booking in. If bookings have recovered and you want the price back up, type the price you want on the calendar, or delete the rule, which undoes every cut it made.

**"Bookings recovered, so why did the cut not come off?"** Because bookings arriving never take a cut off. A cut rule can keep cutting the same night after each wait, down to your floor. Once three of its cuts are on the night the amber banner asks whether it should keep going, and until you answer, it does. Read [Rules that keep adjusting](@43).

When you type a price for a night and room type on the calendar:

- every booking speed and pickup change already on that night and room type comes off ("this night's price was set by hand" in the change log)
- every standard rule change already there is held: the rule stays on, so it does not fire again on the same trigger, but it stops moving the price until its condition next changes
- your number becomes the base, and rules that fire later stack on top of it
- a booking speed or pickup rule that already existed waits its wait, in whole days from the day you saved, then reads its whole window again

Read [Setting a price yourself](@50). Clearing your price hands the night back: held standard rules move the price again, but the booking speed and pickup changes that came off stay off.

**Careful: Typing a price is the quickest undo** · If a price looks wrong and you want it fixed now, type the price you want. It is saved at once. If you are live on Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations it is sent right away or on the next cycle, about five minutes later (the screen says which). A night more than 395 nights ahead is sent when it enters the 396-night window. A 0 is not sent, and nothing is sent to Mews. Read [Undo a price change](@67).

You change a rule with **Edit** and **Save changes**, or by accepting a "Tune ... ?" card after **Get suggestions from my data**, which moves a standard rule's occupancy threshold. What happens to the changes the rule already has on the price depends on how the edit is saved:

| The rule | Saved with **Apply price adjustments** | Saved with **Skip price adjustments** |
|---|---|---|

The window before the save shows the days Apply would change. Read [Turning a rule on, Apply or Skip](@41).

**With Skip, price changes that were on the price** also come off when the night passes, when you type a price on the night, or when you delete the rule. Saving the rule again with **Apply price adjustments** ends the holds, and its changes are judged as Apply judges them.

A new name or the undo box alone leaves the rule's changes where they are (the box then decides about cancellations from the next cycle). An edit saved to a rule that is **Off** changes no price: its changes stay frozen, still cover the rules they covered, and the window when you switch it on shows what the edited rule does. Changing the conditions, amount or room types also clears the rule's "Stop for this night" answers.
With Skip, price changes that were on the price

**"Why did the change log say the rule was edited?"** A booking speed or pickup change that comes off because its rule was edited with Apply reads ""Warm-date bump" stopped applying an earlier 10% raise here: the rule was edited, so MAYA started it fresh." A standard rule's change that comes off reads as any standard rule letting go.
"Why did the change log say the rule was edited?"
Once your property's date moves past a night, every change on it is left as it was and nothing touches it again. Past nights are never re-priced.

Deleting a rule removes every change it made, whether from a standard rule or a booking speed or pickup rule, from the next cycle. Every night it adjusted goes back to what the price would be if the rule had never run. The delete dialog says so and offers **Turn It Off and Keep Its Changes** beside **Delete Rule and Undo Its Changes**. Read [Turning a rule off, deleting it, or changing it](@42).

Turning a rule off undoes nothing: its changes stay exactly as they are, and cancellations do not take them off while it is off.

| What happened | What you read |
|---|---|
| A standard rule switched off | If another rule or a typed price is still on the night, its next entry shows the price without the change, and no rule is named for the drop. If it was the only change: "Busy nights" stopped applying an earlier 10% raise here: this night no longer met its conditions. That took this night from $165.00 to $150.00. |
| A change came off for cancellations | Cancellations meant "Warm-date bump" was no longer true, so its 10% raise came off. Then the numbers the check found, and the move back when nothing else is left on the night |
| You typed a price | "Warm-date bump" stopped applying an earlier 10% raise here: this night's price was set by hand. Then a line naming who set it. |
| A booking speed or pickup rule was edited, with Apply | "Warm-date bump" stopped applying an earlier 10% raise here: the rule was edited, so MAYA started it fresh. |
| A rule was deleted | The next run prices without it. In older entries a deleted standard rule is called "Pricing rule" with no reason given, and a deleted booking speed or pickup rule's line is left out |

**"Why did the price go back to the base rate?"** One of: a standard rule's condition stopped holding, cancellations meant a rule was no longer true, you or a colleague cleared a typed price, an edit to the rule was applied, or the rule was deleted. The change log lists the night in the run that did it: it names what came off, then "That took this night from" the old price to the new one. When another rule or a typed price is still on the night, its entry shows the price without the change, and names a change that came off for cancellations.

**Not yet** · There is no undo button for one price change. The three ways back are: type the price you want on that night (now), delete the rule (undoes everything it did, everywhere), or stop the rule on that night from the banner once three of its changes are on it (no more changes, and what it did stays unless cancellations take it off).

Whenever a rule is about to start acting, a window opens first. It shows a small calendar of the months ahead with the days the rule will change filled in, and a line such as "41 days will be affected by this rule." Click **Apply price adjustments** and the rule changes those days from the next pricing run. Click **Skip price adjustments** and the rule is on, but those days keep their prices until the rule stops being true on a day and then becomes true again. Every other day works as if you had applied it. When nothing would change, the window says "0 prices will be affected by this rule." and **Turn it on** switches it on (**Save changes** saves an edit to a rule that is on). **Cancel** saves nothing.

| What you do | The window |
|---|---|
| Switch a rule **On** in the rules list | Opens, headed "Turn on "Busy nights"?" |
| Click **Add Rule** in the rule builder | Opens, headed "Add "Busy nights"?" (a new rule is saved on) |
| Click **Save changes** on a rule that is on | Opens, headed "Save changes to "Busy nights"?", unless only the name changed |
| Click **Add this rule** or **Make that change** on a card from **Get suggestions from my data** | Opens |
| Switch a rule **Off** | Does not open: switching off is at once, and the rule's changes stay |
| Save a new name alone, or save changes to a rule that is off | Does not open: neither moves a price. An edited rule that is off shows the window when you switch it on |
| Accept a rule card in your first review, or the starter rules | Does not open: the property is being set up |
| **Save This Rule** in the **Rate Simulator** | Does not open: the rule arrives switched off. Switching it on opens the window |

The calendar starts at your property's today and runs to the last night MAYA prices, 395 nights on, a small block per month. That is 13 or 14 months, the first and last blocks usually partly empty, so every day the count includes can be seen. The first block and each January name their year. Each block has a row per week, Sunday first, as on the **Calendar** tab, and one small square per night.

- A filled blue square is a day the rule will change.
- A dark square is a day it will not.
- Today has a thin outline.
- Days before today and after the last priced night are left blank.

Hover a blue square to read the day and how many room types change, such as "Sat 3 Oct 2026: prices change on 2 room types". A screen reader reads the affected days out as runs of dates.

Under the calendar is one line: "41 days will be affected by this rule.", "1 day will be affected by this rule.", or "0 prices will be affected by this rule." A "?" beside it explains the rest.

A day counts when the rule changes the price of at least one room type that night. The days come from a trial run of the same pricing that runs every few minutes, done twice on your bookings as they are right now: once with the rule as you are about to save it, and once as things stand. The two sets of prices are compared night by night, to the cent. So everything else is already taken into account:

- every other rule, including a stronger rule that already covers the night, a rule waiting after its last change, and the one change a booking speed or pickup rule can make on a night per run
- prices you typed, comp nights at 0, and nights left unpriced

**0 prices.** "0 prices will be affected by this rule." means no price moves now: the rule is not true anywhere yet, or where it is, something else holds the price. With nothing to change, applying and skipping come to the same thing, so the window offers one button, **Turn it on**, and **Cancel**. For an edit to a rule that is already on, the button reads **Save changes** instead. Either one saves the rule on, as **Apply price adjustments** does. From then on it acts on what becomes true, and a booking speed or pickup rule counts every booking on the books, the ones made before the rule included. If the days changed while the window was open, the new days show with **Apply price adjustments** and **Skip price adjustments** instead (read [When something changes while it is open](#when-something-changes-while-it-is-open)).
0 prices

**A cut on low pickup with no booking window.** When the rule is **Decrease the rate** with a **Pickup count (advanced)** row set to **Less than** and no **Booking window (days to stay)** row, two amber lines follow the count, worked out in the same trial run: "With no booking window condition, this rule reaches 396 of the 396 nights ahead. A night that gained under 1 room night over the 7 full days before counts as quiet, and a far-out night with no bookings yet always will, once your rules have run for 1 week." and "The cut repeats: each time its wait of 1 week is over and the night is still quiet, it cuts again, on top of the cut before." The first number is every night the rule can act on (fewer when it has a date range or weekdays), the second is the window your rules price, and the amount, lookback and wait are the rule's own.
A cut on low pickup with no booking window

The rule is saved and on. The days in blue are priced first on the next pricing run, about five minutes away, and the rest of the window follows over the next runs. The prices that result are the ones the calendar showed. The **Calendar** tab and the change log show them as they land. In simulation nothing is sent. Live on Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations, the new prices are sent to your property system. On Mews, they change in MAYA only.

After an edit, Apply judges every change the rule already has on the price against the edited rule:

- a standard rule's change stays where the edited rule holds, at the new amount, and comes off where it does not, including on room types taken off the rule and nights the rule no longer covers

The rule is saved and on, and the days in blue keep their prices. On each of those days the rule leaves its part of the price as it is until the rule stops being true there and then becomes true again. From then on it acts on that day as on any other. Every day that is not blue works exactly as if you had clicked **Apply price adjustments**.

- **A standard rule** (occupancy or booking window only): on a blue day where it was about to raise or cut, it is on with no change on the price. Once it stops being true there and later is true again, it adjusts.
A standard rule

- **A booking speed or pickup rule**: on a blue day it makes no change while it stays true. The first time it is true there after not being true, it adjusts, in that same run.

Whether the rule is true on a blue day is read from the night as it is now, whatever its undo box says. The box keeps a change the rule made through cancellations, and on a blue day the rule has made none, so with the box unticked too, cancellations that take a blue day under the rule's occupancy line mean the rule has stopped being true there.
A booking speed or pickup rule

**Counting.** Skip never changes where a rule counts from. A booking speed or pickup rule counts every booking on the books, the ones made before you added it included, whether you applied or skipped. So on a day that was not blue, a booking that arrives after you skip can make the rule adjust on the next run, counted together with the bookings before it.
Counting

**Changes already on the price.** Switching a rule that has changes on the price back on, or saving an edit to a rule that is on, leaves its changes on the blue days where they are:

- a standard rule's change the edit would have moved to the new amount stays at its old amount while the rule is true there, and still stays once it stops being true. The next time the rule is true there, it moves to the rule's amount.
- a standard rule's change the rule would have taken off stays at its amount. Where the rule is not true on that day, it stays until the rule is true there, then moves to the rule's amount, or comes off on a room type or night the rule no longer covers. Where the rule is true there but no longer covers that room type or night, it stays until the rule has stopped being true there and is true again, then comes off.
Changes already on the price

- a booking speed or pickup rule's changes stay, are not checked for cancellations while the day is held, and still count as the newest change on the night where the weaker rules count from. They rank as the rule did when it made them, so an edit that lowers the amount or changes the speed does not change which rules they cover. When the day's hold ends, the changes from before an edit come off and the edited rule adjusts in that same run.

They also come off when the night passes, when you type a price on the night, or when you delete the rule. On days that are not blue, the rule's changes are judged as Apply judges them (read [Apply price adjustments](#apply-price-adjustments)).

**Off and on again.** Switching the rule off freezes it, held days included. Switching it back on opens the window again. With **Apply price adjustments** the held days end: every change the rule has on the price is judged as Apply judges it, so a change still at its old amount moves to the rule's amount, and the window counts those days. With **Skip price adjustments** the days the window shows then are held instead. An edit saved with either choice does the same.
Off and on again

**After a Skip.** Skip itself never changes a price. The prices on the blue days move later only once the rule has stopped and started being true there, or when something else moves them: a price you type, or another rule.

**Example: Skipping at The Harbour Inn**

Priya adds "Busy nights": more than 80% full, raise 10%. The window shows "6 days will be affected by this rule." She clicks **Skip price adjustments**. Friday, 17 of 20 booked, stays at $150 while it stays above 80%. On Saturday, 14 of 20 when she skipped, two bookings arrive and it reaches 16 of 20: Saturday was not blue, so Saturday goes to $165 on the next run. If Friday drops to 15 of 20 and later fills again, Friday gets the raise then.
After a Skip
**Cancel**, the Esc key or a click outside the window saves nothing. A rule you were switching on stays **Off**, and the rule builder keeps everything you typed, so you can change it and try again.

When you click **Apply price adjustments**, **Skip price adjustments**, **Turn it on** or **Save changes**, the save first checks whether anything that could move the days changed since they were worked out: a booking or a cancellation, a price typed, a pricing run, another rule, a room type. If something did, the days are worked out again. When they are the same, the rule is saved straight away, and a Skip holds those days. When they are not, nothing is saved, the calendar and the count show the new days, and a line reads "Your bookings changed while this was open, so the days were checked again." Choose again.

If the check fails or takes too long, the line reads "We weren't able to calculate how many days would be affected by this rule." The window then offers three buttons, and no **Apply price adjustments**, since there is no count to apply:

- **Try again** works the days out again.
- **Skip price adjustments** turns the rule on without changing any price now. With no days to go on, it holds every day the rule could change: each night in its scope and each night with a change of it on the price, each until the rule stops being true there and then becomes true again, as above.
- **Cancel** saves nothing.

When the check was refused because of too many checks at once, "That's a lot of checks at once. Give it a minute and try again." shows under that line.

While the days are worked out, the squares are grey and pulse, the line reads "Checking your calendar…", and the buttons wait. A rule on occupancy or booking window is usually answered within a second or two. A booking speed or pickup rule takes longer, because every night it could act on is priced: its calendar is asked for in three parts at once, the nearest two months first, and the count appears only when all three are in, usually within a few seconds.

Revenue Managers, General Managers and Hotel Admins. For a Viewer the window opens for a moment and closes again, and "Only a Revenue Manager or above can change this." appears under the rule's switch, or under the rule builder. Nothing is saved. Read [Roles: who can do what](@64).

|---|---|---|
| Checking your calendar… | In the window, while the days are worked out | Wait a moment |
| 0 prices will be affected by this rule. | In the window | Click **Turn it on** (**Save changes** for an edit to a rule that is on), or **Cancel** |
| We weren't able to calculate how many days would be affected by this rule. | In the window | Click **Try again**, or **Skip price adjustments**, or **Cancel** |
| Your bookings changed while this was open, so the days were checked again. | In the window, after **Apply price adjustments**, **Skip price adjustments**, **Turn it on** or **Save changes** | Look at the new days and choose again |
