Off freezes: the rule stops acting and the prices it already set stay exactly as they are. Delete undoes: every night it adjusted goes back to what it would have been. **Edit** opens a rule in the rule builder to change any of its settings. Before a rule starts acting, whether you switch it on or save changes to it while it is on, a window shows which days it will change and asks whether to apply or skip the price adjustments.

Each rule on the **Rules** tab has a switch under **Status** that reads **On** or **Off**.

- Switching **Off** is at once, with no confirmation, from the next cycle.
- Switching **On** first opens a window, headed "Turn on "Busy nights"?", with a small calendar of the days the rule will change and "X days will be affected by this rule." Click **Apply price adjustments** and it acts on those days from the next cycle. Click **Skip price adjustments** and it is on, but those days keep their prices until the rule stops being true on a day and then becomes true again; every other day works as with Apply. When no price would change, the window reads "0 prices will be affected by this rule." and **Turn it on** switches it on. **Cancel** leaves it **Off**. Read [Turning a rule on, Apply or Skip](@41).

- a booking speed or pickup rule's raises and cuts stay on the price, and they are not checked for cancellations while it is off
- on the day cards and in your property system, nothing moves

Turn the rule back **On** and the window shows what that changes. With **Apply price adjustments** it picks up from the next cycle: a standard rule that was holding a change lets it go where the condition no longer holds, and the rule acts wherever it holds. With **Skip price adjustments** its changes on the days the window showed stay where they are, each until the rule stops being true there and then becomes true again, and every other night works as with Apply.

- **Delete Rule and Undo Its Changes**: removes the rule and every change it made, from the next cycle
- **Turn It Off and Keep Its Changes**: switches the rule off and closes the dialog
- **Cancel**

The change log keeps its price entries, but older entries lose the deleted rule's reasons. A standard rule's move still shows, named "Pricing rule", with no sentence saying why. A booking speed or pickup rule's move is left out of those entries. Your answers to the rule's keeps-adjusting banner (the "Your answer" entries) are removed along with the rule. New entries show the price without it. Read [The change log](@47).

**Careful** · Deleting a rule changes prices. Every night the rule had adjusted is re-priced without it from the next cycle, nearest nights first. On a live Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations property, those prices are sent to your system. On Mews they change in MAYA only. If you want the prices to stay where they are, turn the rule off instead.

Click **Edit** beside **Delete** at the end of the rule's row. The rule builder opens under the list, headed "Edit "Busy nights"", with the rule as it is saved: its name, its conditions, the direction and amount, the room types it measures and changes, and the undo box, **Undo the change if cancellations mean this rule is no longer true**. The rule's row is highlighted while you edit. Change what you want and click **Save changes**:
- **Only the name changed**: saved at once. A name moves no price.
Only the name changed

- **The rule is On**: the window opens first, headed "Save changes to "Busy nights"?", with the days the edited rule will change. Apply, Skip or Cancel, as for switching a rule on. Cancel keeps what you typed in the builder.
The rule is On

- **The rule is Off**: saved at once, and no price moves. Its changes stay frozen, and the window shows what the edited rule does when you switch it on.

**Cancel editing**, under the form, empties the builder without saving. A rule's date window, weekdays and priority are not in the builder, and an edit keeps them as saved. If someone changed the rule in another tab after you opened it, the save stops with "This rule changed in another tab. Reload it to edit." and a **Reload** button that fills the builder with the rule as it is now.
The rule is Off

**What an edit does to the rule's changes.** With **Apply price adjustments**, every change the rule has on the price is judged against the edited rule: a standard rule's change stays at the new amount where the edited rule holds and comes off where it does not (room types taken off the rule and nights it no longer covers included), and a booking speed or pickup rule's earlier changes come off, with the edited rule reading its whole window again. With **Skip price adjustments**, every change on the days the window showed stays where it is until the rule stops being true there and then becomes true again, and every other night is judged as with Apply. Changing its conditions, amount or room types also clears the rule's "Stop for this night" answers, which belonged to the rule as it was. A new name or the undo box alone keeps them.
What an edit does to the rule's changes

The "Tune ... ?" card after **Get suggestions from my data** is an edit too: **Make that change** moves the occupancy threshold of a standard rule, through the same window when the rule is on. Read [Getting suggestions later](@29) and [Change a rule](@72).

**Not yet** · You cannot copy or duplicate a rule, or copy one to another property. For those, add the rule again. A rule you build in the **Rate Simulator** arrives on the Rules tab switched off.
The rules table has seven columns: **Name**, **Fired**, **Conditions**, **Room Types**, **Price Change**, **Status**, and the **Edit** and **Delete** buttons. On a narrow screen it scrolls sideways.
**Order.** Most fired first, then rules that are on before rules that are off, then by name.
Order
**Filter.** The pills above the table, **All**, **Enabled** and **Disabled**, show every rule, only the ones that are on, or only the ones that are off.
Filter

**Fired.** How many times the rule has acted, counted once per night and room type. A dash means never. A "?" beside the heading explains that a booking speed or pickup rule can act on the same night more than once, and each time counts, and that a change that came off later still counts. So the count is usually higher than the changes you can see on the calendar now, and higher than the change log shows, which lists the 40 biggest moves of each run and only counts the rest.
Fired

**Conditions.** In words: "Occupancy above 80%", "Booking window below 7 days", "Pickup above 5 bookings (past 3 days), then waits 3 days", "booking speed at least Faster Than Normal (past week), then waits 1 week". Several are joined with a dot.
Conditions
**Room Types.** The types the rule changes, or "Watches Standard, Deluxe · Changes Suite" when it measures different ones.
Room Types

**Price Change.** "+10%", "-15%", "+$25", "-$25". The sign in this column is always a dollar sign, whatever your property's currency. The amount is in your currency. The change log and the keeps-adjusting banner use your currency's own symbol.
Price Change
**Stopped on N nights.** An amber chip under the switch when you have told the rule to stop on some upcoming nights, with a "?" and a **Let it run again** link. Read [Rules that keep adjusting](@43).
Stopped on N nights

At most 40 rules can be **On** at once on a property. Rules that are **Off** do not count, and a rule saved from the **Rate Simulator** arrives Off. At 40, the window with the calendar opens for a moment when you add a rule or switch an Off rule on, then closes, and "This property already has 40 active rules, which is the maximum." shows in red under the form or under the rule's switch. Nothing is saved. Turn a rule off or delete one first.

Every occupancy or booking window rule whose condition holds applies, and their changes stack. Booking speed and pickup rules take turns: at most one fires on a night and room type per run. Read [How rules run](@39).

Revenue Managers, General Managers and Hotel Admins can switch, edit and delete rules. A Viewer sees the switch and the **Edit** and **Delete** buttons, and can open a rule in the builder to read it, but switching, saving or deleting changes nothing and shows "Only a Revenue Manager or above can change this." in red under the rule or the form. Read [Roles: who can do what](@64).

The app does not show who added, switched or deleted a rule. If you need to know, [email us](mailto:info@modern-hospitality-solutions.com?subject=Who%20changed%20a%20rule) with the rule's name and roughly when.

The change log has no entry for adding a rule, editing it, switching it on or off, or deleting it, or for which of Apply or Skip was chosen: it shows only what those steps did to prices. The people the change log does name are whoever typed a price ("Priya set the base rate to $180.00.") and whoever answered the keeps-adjusting banner (the "Your answer" entries).

When three of a booking speed or pickup rule's changes are on the same night, an amber banner asks you: keep adjusting, or stop for this night. Until you answer, it keeps going. Stop means no more changes there, and what it already did stays. You can let it run again from the **Rules** tab.

A booking speed or pickup rule fires, waits, and can fire again on the same night. Each fire stacks on the last, so a night can climb (or fall) a long way on one rule. So at three, MAYA asks you.

The count is per rule, per night: the most of its changes still on the price on any one of that night's room types. The banner warns how far the price can go, so a change that has come off, for cancellations or because you typed a price, does not count. Only booking speed and pickup rules can reach three. A standard rule fires once per change of state.

The rule does not stop at three. It keeps firing after its wait, as usual, until you answer. The banner is your chance to say otherwise.

The banner appears a few minutes after the third change. It does not refresh by itself, so reload the page to see the latest.

It sits above the tab content on every tab, in amber, and opens straight with the rule's headline. One card per rule, rules A to Z. Each card has:

- **A headline.** "Hot-week surge" has 3 raises on Fri, Nov 13 2026. For several nights: "Slow-date rescue" has 3 cuts on each of 4 nights (or "3 to 5 cuts"). When a night's room types have different counts, it says "up to": "up to 3 raises", or "up to 5 cuts on each of 4 nights".
A headline
- **A consequence line.** "It keeps raising these nights until you stop it."
A consequence line

- **One block per night.** The night, then how many changes are on each room type ("3 raises on Standard and 1 raise on Deluxe"), then what the rule saw at its latest fire: "In the 7 days it measured, 9 bookings came in. A night like this usually has about 4 by then." or, for a pickup rule, "Pickup over the last 3 days came to 6 room nights, against the 4 you set." When the rule counted from its earlier raise, or a stronger rule's, the line opens "Since the raise before its latest one, by it or a stronger rule," instead.
One block per night

- **A limit line.** Where the price can go if the rule carries on: "If it keeps cutting, the price can fall to your $80.00 floor for Standard." When the limit is still the default: "Your ceiling for Suite is still MAYA's $99,999.99 default, so the price can climb that far." with a "?" and a link, **Ask MAYA for a ceiling** or **Ask MAYA for a floor**, which takes you to the **Rules** tab and its **Get suggestions from my data** button. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).

Prices in the banner use your property's currency symbol.
A limit line

It keeps raising these nights until you stop it.

Sat, Nov 14 2026 · 3 raises on Standard, 3 raises on Deluxe and 2 raises on Suite

"Slow-date trim" waits a week, so at its third trim it counted the 6 full days after the day of its second: "In the 6 days it measured". A rule that raises on a fast pace, such as "Hot-week surge", names the raise instead, and sets those bookings against a whole week of a similar night. Read [Counting after a rule acts](@35#counting-after-a-rule-acts).
"Why does it say 3 days when my rule measures the past week?"

To keep a night's price where it is, type the price and switch off the rules that would move it. Switching off stops a rule on every night, not only this one, so switch it back on once the night has passed.

Make up a night: a stay date, a booking speed level, and each room type's base price, occupancy and pickup. The simulator runs your real rules with the same maths a real run uses and shows what each room type becomes and why. Nothing is saved and nothing is sent. A test rule you build here can be saved to the **Rules** tab, switched off.

The **Rate Simulator** tab (the third tab on the dashboard) answers "what would my rules do to a night like this?" without waiting for such a night to come along. Its own words: "Make up a night and see what your rules would do to it. Nothing here is saved and no rate reaches your PMS." It adds: "The math is the same a real run uses, so what you see is what your rules would produce for these numbers."

Use it to check a rule before you build it, to see which of two rules would act, or to see why a price on the calendar is what it is. Everyone on the property can use it.

While it loads it reads "Loading this property's rooms and rules...". Before your first sync it says the property has no active room types yet, and asks you to connect a system and finish the import first.

Under **The night**:

- **Stay date**, starting 30 days ahead. The note under it says the date sets the days to arrival. They are counted from your property's date, not your computer's, so the number matches what a real run would see, and a booking window rule reads it.
- **Booking speed**, a dropdown with **Not enough history** and the seven levels: Stalled, Much Slower Than Normal, Slower Than Normal, Normal, Faster Than Normal, Much Faster Than Normal, Surging. It starts on **Not enough history**, and the note says booking speed rules then stay quiet, and that the math is the same a real run uses: a real run keeps them quiet too when there isn't enough history to read a pace. Pick a level to test a booking speed rule. A made-up night has no bookings to count, so the level you pick is taken as read.

One row per room type that counts as a room, with its room count under its name. Room types you have unticked as rooms are not here.

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Base price** | The price rules start from. It opens on the nearest price MAYA has published for that room type. With none published yet, it opens halfway between the floor and the ceiling when the ceiling is at most 10 times the floor, otherwise on the floor. |
| **Occupancy** | A percentage from 0 to 100, starting at 70. Beside it, "(8 of 12)" shows how many rooms that is, out of the full room count. Rooms out of service are not taken off here. |
| **Picked up** | Rooms gained over a pickup rule's lookback, starting at 0. A pickup rule that measures revenue values each one at the base price. |
| **Guardrails** | The room type's floor and ceiling, for reference. You cannot change them here. |

An occupancy rule reads occupancy across the room types it measures, added together. Two room types at 92% and 50% with 12 and 6 rooms read as 14 of 18, which is 78%. The rule checks its conditions once, on that one figure, so it fires on every room type it changes or on none of them.

Every rule on the property is listed with a checkbox, all ticked. Untick one to leave it out of the run. Beside each name:

- "ladder" or "event": the simulator's own words for the two kinds of rule. "ladder" is a standard rule (only occupancy and booking window conditions), which holds one change while its condition holds. "event" is a booking speed or pickup rule, which fires, keeps its change and can fire again after its wait. The rest of these docs say "standard rule" and "booking speed and pickup rules".
- "off" when the rule is switched off on the **Rules** tab
- "fires" when it fires on the night you have set up
- "Watches Standard, Deluxe · Changes Suite" when the rule measures different room types from the ones it changes

Click **+ Build a test rule** and a smaller rule builder opens:

- **Rule name**. An unnamed draft is called "Unsaved test rule".
- Up to 4 conditions under "When all of these are true", one of each kind, each with a **Metric**, an **Is** dropdown (**above** or **below**) and a **Value**. A **Booking speed (recommended)** row has a **Speed** dropdown with the seven levels instead. The metric labels differ slightly from the main builder: **Occupancy (%)** here is **Sellable occupancy (%)** there. The others match.
- **Then** (**raise the rate** or **lower the rate**), **By** and **Unit** (**percent** or **dollars**).
- The undo box, **Undo the change if cancellations mean this rule is no longer true**, ticked to start. It is saved with the rule. Nothing cancels on a made-up night, so it does not change what the table shows.
- **Room types**, as pills, all on to start.

**Save This Rule** saves it to the **Rules** tab switched off, and the screen reads "Rule Added to Rules Tab and Initialized as Disabled". Turn it on from the **Rules** tab when you are ready: the switch first shows the days it will change, and you apply or skip the price adjustments. To change it first, click **Edit** on its row. Read [Try a rule before turning it on](@80).

The button stays greyed out until the draft has a condition, an amount and at least one room type. An amount of 0 (or a blank **By** box) cannot be saved: the save fails with an error. Type a real amount. Saving needs Revenue Manager access or higher: a Viewer who presses it sees an error.

**Good to know: No Measured over or Then waits here** · The test-rule builder has no **Measured over** or **Then waits (advanced)** fields. A booking speed test rule is saved with the defaults: **Past week** and a wait of **1 week**. A pickup test rule is saved with a 3-day lookback measuring room nights, and waits the same as its lookback. For other settings, build the rule on the **Rules** tab instead. [The rule builder, field by field](@31) covers every field.

The results table has one row per room type: **Room type**, **Base**, **Becomes**, **Change** (the move in money, or a dash for none) and **Because**.

- **Becomes** is the price after every rule that fires and after the floor and ceiling. A "held at your floor" or "held at your ceiling" tag shows when a limit stepped in, and **Because** adds what the rules asked for, such as "Rules asked for $412.50."
- **Because** names each rule that fired, with "(currently off)" beside a rule that is off on the **Rules** tab, or reads "No rule fires on this night".

Under the table, **Didn't fire** lists each rule that did not fire and why:

| Reason | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Conditions not met (it saw 62% occupancy, 30 days out) | The night does not meet the rule's conditions. The numbers are what the rule read. |
| No occupancy for its signal room types | None of the room types the rule measures is in the table, so it has nothing to read. |
| Rule has no room types attached | The rule changes no room type. |
| Outside the rule's date window, or This day of the week is excluded | You will not see these for a rule you built in MAYA: every rule you build runs every day with no date window. A starter rule whose name ends in "(Fri and Sat)" or "(Sun to Thu)" shows "This day of the week is excluded" on the other nights. |

Amounts in the simulator carry your property's currency sign, the same one the change log's sentences use.

**Example: Testing 'Last minute' at The Harbour Inn**

Priya wants to see "Last minute" (**Booking window (days to stay)** **Less than** 3 and **Sellable occupancy (%)** **Less than** 50, **Decrease the rate** 15%) act. It measures and changes all three room types. She sets **Stay date** to tomorrow, then Standard to $150 at 40% (5 of 12), Deluxe to $200 at 30% (2 of 6) and Suite to $300 at 50% (1 of 2).

"Last minute" reads one figure for the three types together: 8 of 20 rooms, which is 40%. That is less than 50, so it fires on every room type. Standard becomes $127.50, Deluxe $170.00 and Suite $255.00.

She changes Deluxe to 100%. Now the rule reads 12 of 20, which is 60%, so it fires on none of them and all three stay at their base. **Didn't fire** reads: Last minute, Conditions not met (it saw 60% occupancy, 1 days out).

"Busy nights" (occupancy **Greater than** 80, Increase 10%) fires on every room type. "Warm-date bump" (**Faster Than Normal** or above, Increase 10%) fires too. Standard becomes $181.50 (150, then 165, then 181.50). Deluxe becomes $242.00. Suite becomes $363.00, well under its $600 ceiling.

She switches booking speed to **Not enough history**. "Warm-date bump" moves to **Didn't fire** with "Conditions not met", and Standard becomes $165.00.

The math is the same a real run uses, but a real night plays out over days and this is one run. The note at the bottom of the results says so, starting "The math is the same a real run uses, but this preview simplifies three things". In plain words:
- **A standard rule is shown settled.** On a real night it fires on the way into its condition and holds. Here you see where the night ends up, not each step.
A standard rule is shown settled

- **Every matching booking speed or pickup rule is added.** On a real night, when several booking speed or pickup rules match, one wins for that night and room type. Here they all fire, so the result is the most the night could move.
Every matching booking speed or pickup rule is added
- **A repeat is shown once.** A booking speed or pickup rule that is still true after its wait adjusts the night again on a real night. Here it fires once.
A repeat is shown once

- **Booking speed is a level you chose,** not a count against similar nights, so there is no "Show the numbers" behind it.

The screen sums it up: "It is one run, not where a night ends up over a week." [How rules run](@39) explains what happens across a week.

**Not yet** · The simulator cannot replay a real past run, and it cannot count bookings: booking speed is a level you pick. To see what really happened on a night, read the change log entry for it and open **Show the numbers**. Read [The change log](@47).
Booking speed is a level you chose,

Rules you build run every day of the year, for every night in the window. When two rules compete, the stronger one, the one that changes the price by more, fires. You cannot yet limit a rule to weekends, a date range, a season or some channels, set which rule wins, edit a rule, make an either/or rule, set an exact price, or cap how far prices move. Here is what to do instead.

**A weekend-only rule.** Every rule you build runs every day of the week. There is no weekday choice in the builder, and MAYA has no setting for which nights are your weekend. (In these docs, and in how similar nights are chosen, weekends are Friday and Saturday nights.) The one kind of rule limited to some days is a starter rule copied from your own rates after you answered "My pricing works": when you made a move only on Friday and Saturday nights, or only on the others, its name ends in "(Fri and Sat)" or "(Sun to Thu)". Read [Your starter rules](@27#if-you-picked-my-pricing-works). What to do instead: for a weekend price, type a price on those nights on the calendar. It becomes the base for that night, and the rules already on it are held (their changes come off). Read [Setting a price yourself](@50).
A weekend-only rule

**A date range, a season or an event.** Every rule runs for every night in the 396-night window, all year. What to do instead: for a wedding weekend or a festival, type a price for the range with **through…** on the calendar (up to 366 nights in one save, from tonight to 399 days ahead). Rules already on those nights are held (their changes come off), and rules that fire later stack on top, so switch off the rules that would move those nights until the weekend has passed. Switching a rule off stops it on every night, so switch it back on afterwards. Read [Hold a price for a wedding or event weekend](@68). For seasons, booking speed already compares inside the season your history shows, so a booking speed rule adjusts to the season by itself.
A date range, a season or an event

**Priority.** There is no priority control. When two booking speed or pickup rules are true on the same night, the stronger one fires: the one that changes the price by more, then, at the same change, the one that watches booking speed (set to the faster speed, or the slower one for cuts), then the pickup count harder to meet. Only after those do the five starter rules rank above yours, then the rule with more conditions, then the older rule. Standard rules do not compete: every one whose condition holds applies. Read [How rules run](@39#which-one-fires-when-several-match).
Priority

**Editing a rule.** You can: **Edit** on the rule's row opens it in the rule builder, name and undo box included. What an edit cannot reach is what the builder has no field for: a date window, weekdays or a priority. Read [Change a rule](@72).
Editing a rule

**Either/or.** Conditions on one rule are always "and": "Matches when all of the following are true." For "busy or last-minute", make two rules. Both can act on the same night, and their changes stack.
Either/or
**One night only.** A rule cannot be limited to one night. Type a price for that night instead.
One night only
**Both a percent and a fixed amount.** A rule has one amount: type a number in one box and the other greys out. For "10% plus $5", make two rules. They stack.
Both a percent and a fixed amount

**An exact price, like $199.** A rule changes the price by a percent or a fixed amount, up or down. It cannot set the price to a number. For an exact price, type it on the calendar for that night, or for a run of nights with **through…**. It is published as you typed it, and rules that fire later stack on top of it. Read [Setting a price yourself](@50).
An exact price, like $199
**Copy or duplicate a rule, or copy rules to another property.** Not yet. Build the rule again. Rules belong to one property.
Copy or duplicate a rule, or copy rules to another property

**An occupancy threshold above 100.** The measured number can go above 100% (rooms out of service after a night sold, or overbooking), but a threshold above 100 is saved as 100. **Greater than** 100 fires on any overbooked night.
An occupancy threshold above 100

**Two conditions of the same kind.** One of each: at most one occupancy row, one booking speed row, one booking window row and one pickup row per rule. For a band such as "between 60% and 80%", the builder cannot say it. Use two rules: one at **Greater than** 60, and a second at **Greater than** 80 that makes the change you want above the band. The two stack, so choose the second amount with the first already applied.

**Example: A band with two rules**

You want Standard ($150) up $15 above 60% full, and up $30 in all above 80%. Fixed amounts add, so build two rules on Standard alone. Rule A: **Greater than** 60, **Increase the rate**, **Adjust by fixed amount ($)** 15. Rule B: the same with **Greater than** 80. With 9 of 12 Standard rooms booked (75%), only rule A holds: $165. With 11 of 12 booked (92%), both hold: $180.
Two conditions of the same kind

**A cap on how far or how fast prices move.** There is no setting such as "never more than 20% below my base rate" or "at most one change a day", and a floor or ceiling cannot be a percentage. Floors and ceilings are fixed amounts, one pair per room type, the same on every night.

To keep Standard ($150) within 20% of its usual rate, it needs a $120 floor. [Email us](mailto:info@modern-hospitality-solutions.com?subject=Floor%20for%20one%20room%20type) to set it for Standard alone. Answering the floor question again would put $120 on every room type, Deluxe and Suite included. A floor is one amount for every night, so it does not follow a base rate that changes through the year. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28#where-they-are-set).

What holds prices back today:

- the floor and ceiling of each room type
A cap on how far or how fast prices move

- in each cycle, at most one booking speed or pickup rule changes a given night and room type
- once three of a booking speed or pickup rule's changes are on the same night, an amber banner asks you whether it should keep going

A price can still change more than once in a day. A standard rule switches on and off as bookings come and go, and a stronger rule can step in while a weaker one waits. Read [How rules run](@39) and [Floors and ceilings](@28).

**A smallest change, such as "do not send moves under 1%".** There is no minimum-change setting. Any price that changed, even by a cent, is sent to Cloudbeds or ThinkReservations once you are live. What to do instead: use larger amounts, or fewer rules that stack.
A smallest change, such as "do not send moves under 1%"

**No changes in the last few days before arrival, or at certain hours.** There is no freeze window and no quiet hours. Cycles run about every five minutes, day and night, and tonight is always priced. What you can do:

- On a booking speed or pickup rule you build, add a **Booking window (days to stay)** row set to **Greater than** 2. The rule then makes no new change on tonight or the next two nights. What it already did there stays, though with its undo box ticked a change still comes off when cancellations mean the rule is no longer true.
- On a standard rule, the same row takes the rule's change off as the night comes within those days, and that is itself a price change. A standard rule cannot be held still near arrival this way.
No changes in the last few days before arrival, or at certain hours

- A price you type for those nights is published as typed, but rules that fire later still stack on it, so it is not a freeze either.

**Only direct bookings, or leaving out booking sites.** There is no channel filter. Every booking counts the same, whatever channel it came from: direct, through an online travel agency (a booking site), or made at the front desk. That goes for sellable occupancy, booking speed and pickup count alike.
Only direct bookings, or leaving out booking sites

**Length of stay (LOS) pricing, such as cheaper for a 7-night stay.** There is no condition for how long a guest is staying, and no minimum stay setting. MAYA writes one nightly rate per room type on Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations, and nothing to Mews. What to do instead: keep length-of-stay prices and minimum stays in your property system. A long-stay or discounted rate plan set up there to follow your base rate moves by your system's own rules when MAYA changes the base. Read [Prices are not reaching your property system](@100) for how a plan that follows the base rate behaves.
Length of stay (LOS) pricing, such as cheaper for a 7-night stay

**A setting for how bold MAYA is.** There is no aggressiveness setting and no slider from careful to bold. How far and how often prices move depends only on what you set: the rules, their amounts, the speed levels, the waits, and each room type's floor and ceiling. To be bolder, pick larger amounts, levels nearer Normal (such as **Faster Than Normal**), shorter waits or a higher ceiling. To be gentler, do the opposite or raise the floor. The last of the five questions picks your starter rules: copies of the raises and cuts your own rates made, or the usual five with bigger raises where your nights filled early. It sets no boldness for rules you build. Read [The five questions](@25) and [Your starter rules](@27).
A setting for how bold MAYA is

**A rule that raises only when a night is nearly full and booking fast.** This one you can do: put a **Sellable occupancy (%)** row and a **Booking speed (recommended)** row on the same rule. Both must be true.
A rule that raises only when a night is nearly full and booking fast

- Floors and ceilings are per room type, not per night, season or weekend. Read [Floors and ceilings](@28).
- Rooms out of service take rooms off the sellable count for a stretch of nights, which changes what occupancy rules see. Read [Room types and rooms out of service](@52).
- Which room types count as rooms is set on the **PMS** tab.

**Good to know** · Most limits on this page are limits of the rule builder, not of the pricing. A price you type on the calendar can set an exact number, a weekend price or an event price for the nights you choose, and rules keep working around it.

Each day on the calendar shows sellable occupancy for the whole property, rooms booked over rooms you can sell, the room revenue already on the books, and a colour bar that compares the night with your own other nights. Click a day to see every room type's current price and to type a price yourself. The calendar updates on its own as bookings and prices change.
The **Calendar** tab is the first tab on the dashboard and the one MAYA opens on. Everyone on the property can see it, whatever their role.

Across the top you have **Prev** and **Next**, which step one month at a time, and two dropdowns, **Month** and **Year**. The years on offer run from the first month that has any booking or any published price to the last one. A property with no bookings or prices yet sees only the year on screen. **Prev** and **Next** still move across years.

You can open any month, past or future. What changes far ahead is not the calendar but the prices: your rules run on tonight and the next 395 nights, so nights beyond that show no current price (see "When a night has no current price" below).

On the right, once the month has loaded, a small line reads "Updated 3:05:12 PM · live". The time is your browser's clock, to the second, not the property's. Before the month loads it reads "Loading…".

The month is laid out seven days wide with Sunday in the first column. There is no row of weekday names above the grid. Count from the left with Sunday first, or click a day: the heading of the day detail names the weekday.

While the month loads, or while you switch property, a grey placeholder of the same shape stands in for the grid.

Every day is a button. From top to bottom it shows:

| Line | What it is |
|---|---|
| The day number | The date within the month. |
| A large percentage, such as **60%** | Sellable occupancy for the whole property: rooms booked divided by rooms you can sell that night, rounded to a whole percent. |
| "12/20 rooms" | Rooms booked, then rooms you can sell that night. |
| The revenue figure, such as "$2.2k" or "€850" | Room revenue on the books for that night, with your currency's sign. From 1,000 it is shortened to thousands with one decimal. Hover it and the label reads "Room revenue (booked nights)". |
| A thin colour bar | Green, amber or red, comparing the night with your other nights (next section). |

Two details behind those numbers matter when you check them against your property system.

**Only room types ticked as rooms are counted** in the percentage and in "12/20 rooms". A meeting room or a court that you have unticked under **Counts as a room** is left out of both. Rooms you have entered as out of service come off the sellable count for those nights. The Harbour Inn has 20 rooms across Standard, Deluxe and Suite. With 2 Standard rooms out of service and 11 rooms booked, the card reads "11/18 rooms" and 61%.
Only room types ticked as rooms are counted

**The revenue figure sums every room type**, including ones that do not count as rooms. Each booked night is valued at the rate MAYA imported with the booking, or at its current rate if none was imported.
The revenue figure sums every room type

**ThinkReservations:** The room charges ThinkReservations lists for the booking, after discounts, one night at a time. Other lines on the booking, such as separate tax, fee or extra lines, are not in it.

**Mews:** The booking's total price, taxes included, split evenly across its nights. Anything else Mews includes in that total, such as extras, is in it too.

So the figure will not match a revenue report in your system that adds taxes, fees or extras, takes off commission, or reflects a booking's rate after it was changed. A $0 comp or house-use booking adds nothing and lowers the ADR. [Occupancy looks wrong](@99) covers the occupancy side.
What that rate includes depends on your system

**A booking with no amount at all counts as 0.** That happens only when your system reports a booking with no amount on it. The booking still counts as booked, but it adds nothing to the night's revenue or to that room type's Revenue in the day detail, and it lowers that room type's ADR the way a comp booking at 0 does.

**Good to know** · Occupancy on the day card can read over 100%. That happens when rooms were sold before a block or an out of service stretch was entered, or when your system has taken an overbooking. [Occupancy looks wrong](@99) has the detail.
A booking with no amount at all counts as 0

Under the grid a legend names the three colours: "strong night" (green), "typical night" (amber) and "weak night" (red). The legend goes on to say the colour is measured by revenue per room, relative to the property's own results, and that future nights compare against other upcoming nights.

Here is how the colour is set:

- For each night, MAYA adds up the latest rate it has read for each booked room. A booked room with no rate adds nothing.
- It divides that total by the number of rooms in room types that count as rooms. That is revenue per room.
- Nights before today are compared only with other past nights. Today and later are compared only with other upcoming nights. Revenue for a future night keeps growing as bookings land, so mixing the two would paint every future night red.

- Nights inside a closed period you confirmed on the review are left out when the thirds are worked out, but they still get a colour.

The total behind the colour can differ from the revenue figure on the day card. The card uses the rate MAYA imported with each booking, so the two differ when a booking's rate has changed in your system since it was imported.

The colour is not occupancy. A night can be 90% full and still red if those rooms sold cheaply against your other nights, and a half-full night with strong rates can be green.

**Good to know: Colours can lag by a few minutes** · The booked counts and revenue figures are always fresh, but a new booking can take up to 5 minutes to change a colour.

Clicking a day opens a panel under the grid. The clicked day gets a blue ring.

The heading is the full date, for example "Friday, November 13, 2026". Under it, one summary line:

"12/20 rooms · 60% sellable occupancy · revenue on the books $2,180.00"

For a night that has passed, the last part reads "revenue $2,180.00" instead of "revenue on the books". The amount here is the same figure as on the day card, shown in full.

Then one card per active room type, including types that do not count as rooms. Each card shows:

| Line | What it is |
|---|---|
| The room type's name | With a badge beside it when a manual price is open on that night (below). |
| "Booked 8/12" | Rooms booked in this type, then rooms you can sell in this type that night. |
| "ADR $160.00" | ADR means average daily rate: this type's room revenue for the night divided by the rooms booked. When **Booked** reads 0 there is nothing to average, and the line reads "ADR –". |
| "Current price $165.00" | The price your rules produce for this room type on this night, within your floor and ceiling. On Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations, this is the price MAYA sends when you are live (except a price of 0, a comp night). Nothing is sent to Mews. On a night that has passed, it is the last price the night had. It shows a dash when no price has been published (next section). |
| "Revenue $1280.00" | Room revenue on the books for this type on this night. The card prints it without a thousands comma. |
| A price box, **through…**, **Save** and a **?** | The manual price editor. [Setting a price yourself](@50) explains every part of it. |

Amounts on the calendar carry your property's currency sign: $ for US dollars, € for euros, £ for pounds, and the three-letter code in front of the amount for any other currency, such as "CAD 150.00". That is the grid, the summary line, the room type cards, their badges and the price box. It is the same sign the change log's sentences use. The Harbour Inn is in US dollars, so the examples here show $.

**Example: The Harbour Inn on a Friday in November**

Friday, November 13, 2026 has 12 of 20 rooms booked, so the day card reads 60% and "12/20 rooms". Standard has 8 of 12 booked at $160 a night on average, Deluxe 3 of 6 at $200, Suite 1 of 2 at $300, and the Meeting Room is unbooked. Revenue on the books is $1,280 + $600 + $300 = $2,180, so the day card reads "$2.2k" and the day detail "$2,180.00".

The Meeting Room's rate in Cloudbeds is $90, and no rule changes it. Its card reads "Booked 0/1", "ADR –", "Current price $90.00" and "Revenue $0.00". With nothing booked there is no average rate, so the ADR line shows a dash.

Not counting as a room does not stop a type being priced: the Meeting Room starts from its $90 like any other type. Had its rate in Cloudbeds been 0, the night would be closed, and "Current price" would show a dash.

When a manual price is open on a room type for that night, a small amber badge sits beside the room type's name:

- "Manual · $180.00" for a price someone typed in MAYA. Hover it and you see "Set" followed by the date and time it was typed.
- "Changed in Cloudbeds · $180.00" (or "Changed in Think Reservations · ...") for a rate you changed in your property system on a night MAYA had already sent to. Hover it and you see "Seen" followed by the date and time MAYA read it.

**Cloudbeds:** Both badges can appear. The second needs the property to be live and the night to have been sent to and confirmed at least an hour earlier. [Rates you change in your property system](@51) has the conditions.

The badge and the manual price help name your system from your connection, which MAYA reads when the dashboard opens. With no connection on file, or for a moment while the dashboard opens, they say "your PMS" instead.

A dash after "Current price" means MAYA has not published a price for that room type on that night. There are four ordinary reasons:

- **The night is beyond the window.** Your rules run on tonight and the next 395 nights (396 nights, about 13 months). A night further out has no price until it enters the window. A manual price you saved further ahead shows with its badge, and is priced once its night enters the window.
The night is beyond the window

- **The night is closed in your system, or has no rate to start from.** On Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations, a night whose rate in your system is 0, with no manual price typed in MAYA, is left unpriced on purpose. So is a night your system has no rate for at all, for example one further ahead than you have loaded rates: the card reads "No rate in Cloudbeds for this night yet" under the dash, and the "?" beside it says what to do. Load a rate there and the next hourly read picks it up, or type a price in MAYA. A booking's rate is never a starting point. On Mews, MAYA does not read rates, so a night is priced only once you type a price for it.
The night is closed in your system, or has no rate to start from
- **The night has passed and had no price.** A night that has passed is not priced again. The card keeps the last price the night had before it passed, or a dash if it had none.
The night has passed and had no price

- **No run has happened yet.** A newly connected property shows dashes until its first pricing run.

The price your rules start from (the base price) is not shown on the day card. The change log names it in every change: "from $150.00 to $165.00".
No run has happened yet

The calendar updates on its own, within a few seconds of a change to a booking, a published price, a manual price or an out of service block. While the history import is running it refreshes less often, so the page stays calm.

Behind that, while you are on the **Calendar** tab, MAYA re-reads the month every 5 minutes, and again whenever you come back to the browser tab. After you save or clear a manual price the calendar refreshes at once. A month you opened a moment ago can show from memory when you step back to it.

The "· live" marker shows whenever the month has loaded.

**Good to know** · A new booking in your property system reaches MAYA on the next read of your bookings, about every five minutes. So the calendar can show it within about five minutes of the booking, not the same second.

Your rules run in your property's own time zone: "tonight" is today's date there, and that is where the 396-night window starts. The "Updated 3:05:12 PM" time is your browser's clock.

**Example: Why does yesterday still say "revenue on the books"?**

The day detail's summary line switches from "revenue on the books" to "revenue" at midnight UTC (the world reference time), not at midnight at your property. In the Americas that is the afternoon or evening, 4 PM in winter and 5 PM in summer at The Harbour Inn, so tonight can already read "revenue". In most of Europe, and in Asia and Australia, it comes after your own midnight, so yesterday can still read "revenue on the books" for a few hours. Only the label changes, never a number.

**Not yet** · There is no row of weekday names above the grid, no list or week view, and no export. The day card does not show the base price a rule started from, and it does not list the bookings behind a night. To see a night's bookings, open your property system.

The **Change Log** tab shows your 10 most recent pricing runs that changed a price, newest first, however long ago they ran. Each listed night shows its starting price and new price, then plain sentences saying what each rule on it did and why. A price going back to its starting point is listed too, with what came off. The runs in between that changed nothing are counted, not listed: **Show All Cycles** shows each stretch of them as one line, such as "Prices checked 47 times, nothing needed to change".

A pricing run is one pass of MAYA over your property: it reads your bookings, runs every rule that is on against the nights that need it, and publishes a new price wherever one changed. The nights that need it are every night whose bookings changed since the last run and every night a change of yours reaches, and, in the first runs after midnight at your property, every night in the window (tonight and the next 395 nights), nearest first. A run where nothing needed pricing still counts as a run that changed nothing. When you are live, the changed prices are then sent to your property system. In simulation the run happens in full and the log fills in the same way, but nothing is sent.

Runs happen:
- **About every five minutes**, each time MAYA's scheduled read of your bookings succeeds. A read that fails prices nothing that time, and a property whose subscription has lapsed is skipped.
About every five minutes
- **Straight after you save or clear a manual price**, on the nights you saved.
Straight after you save or clear a manual price

- **Straight after you change a room type** (ticking or unticking **Counts as a room**, adding or clearing rooms out of service): the change asks for a run at once. Rooms out of service re-price their own nights. A room type setting re-prices every night in the window over that run and the next few, nearest first.

A run that finds nothing to change is counted into a quiet line between the runs that did. **Show All Cycles** shows those lines.
Straight after you change a room type

- **Show Changes Only** is what the button says once you have opened the full view. The full view adds the quiet lines. Each counts a stretch of runs in a row that changed nothing, with when the first and last of them ran, in small grey type: "Prices checked 47 times from Sep 24, 10:05 AM to 1:55 PM (4 min ago), nothing needed to change." A stretch of one reads "Prices checked once at Sep 24, 1:55 PM". The line under the oldest change shown starts "Just before that, prices were checked 12 times".

When no run has changed a price yet, the default view shows no runs at all, and no message says why. Any "Prices not reaching" problem and any answer you gave still show. Click **Show All Cycles** to see the quiet lines.

Under the heading sits the **Your corrections** panel, closed by default. It lists the past nights you have set aside as not a fair comparison. [Setting a date aside](@49) explains it.

If the log cannot load you see "Couldn't load your price history." with a **Try again** link. Whatever had loaded before stays on screen.

Each run is a box. The first line reads:

"Pricing run · Fri, Oct 2, 2026, 3:05 PM PDT (4 min ago)"

The time is shown in your browser's time zone, with the zone's abbreviation, so two people in different places see different clock times for the same run. Hover the line and the exact moment shows, to the second, on the same clock: "Oct 2, 2026, 3:05:12 PM PDT". The part in brackets says how long ago: "just now", "4 min ago", "2 hr ago", "yesterday", "3 days ago", up to 6 days. Older runs carry no bracket.

Under the first line comes the list of changes, the biggest moves first. A run that made more than 40 changes lists its 40 biggest and ends with a line counting the rest, such as "And 23 more changes in this run."

Each change starts with a bold line:

"Standard · stay 2026-11-13: $150.00 up to $165.00 (+10%)"

That is the room type, the stay night, the night's starting point, the price the run published, and the whole move between those two as a percentage. A cut reads "down to" with a negative percentage.

The starting point is the night's price before any rule: your own rate for that night, or a price someone set (on Mews, always a price someone set). It is not the price the night had before this run. So when a second rule stacks on a night an earlier run already raised from $150.00 to $165.00, the bold line still starts from $150.00:

"Standard · stay 2026-11-13: $150.00 up to $206.25 (+37.5%)"

1. **What came off.** If cancellations took a change off (the rule's undo box is ticked), that comes first: Cancellations meant "Warm-date bump" was no longer true, so its 10% raise came off. The next sentence gives the numbers the check found, such as: Of the 9 bookings it counted, 4 are still booked, where nights like it usually get about 5, and the rule needs a booking speed of at least faster than normal. A change taken off by a typed price reads "Warm-date bump" stopped applying an earlier 10% raise here: this night's price was set by hand.
What came off

2. **Each rule on the price, then why.** Every rule still applying to the night is listed, not only the one that acted in this run. The first reads "Warm-date bump" raised this night 10%, from $150.00 to $165.00. A second rule on the same night reads Then "Hot-week surge" raised it 25%, from $165.00 to $206.25. The "from" price of each later rule is the price the earlier one left, which is how stacking shows itself.
Each rule on the price, then why
3. **The limit, if one stepped in.** That would have gone past your $300.00 ceiling for Standard, so it stopped there.
The limit, if one stepped in

When the run put the night back at its starting point, with nothing left on it, the entry names what came off and ends with the move: "That took this night from $165.00 to $150.00." Its bold line starts from the price the night had before, "Standard · stay 2026-11-13: $165.00 down to $150.00 (-9.1%)". A standard rule that switched off reads "Busy nights" stopped applying an earlier 10% raise here: this night no longer met its conditions. A cleared price reads "The price set by hand was cleared." And a night with nothing on it whose starting point moved reads "The base rate for this night changed from $150.00 to $160.00."

Only one booking speed or pickup rule can fire on a night for one room type in one run. So when two are listed, the first fired on an earlier run and still applies. Its reason then carries no numbers, because those were read on the run it fired.
A fallback

Under the sentences, a change carries a **Show the numbers** button when the run read booking speed for that night. With a booking speed rule that measures the whole property (every booking speed starter rule does), that is nearly every change, whichever rule made it, typed prices included. [The numbers behind a change](@48) covers what it opens.
Every "why" sentence is built from your own rule: the mark you typed, the room types it measures, and the numbers the run saw. The shapes below use The Harbour Inn's rules.

These two share one sentence, because you set them as one condition.

| Rule | Sentence |
|---|---|
| Occupancy Greater than 80 | It was 85% full, past the 80% mark you set. |
| Occupancy Less than 50 | It was 40% full, under the 50% mark you set. |
| Booking window Less than 3 | It had 2 days to go, past the 3-day mark you set. |
| Booking window Greater than 21 | It had 30 days to go, beyond the 21-day mark you set. |
| Both, "Last minute" | It was 40% full with 2 days to go, under the 50% mark and past the 3-day mark you set. |
| Measuring other room types than it changes | Standard and Deluxe were 83% full, past the 80% mark you set. |
| No numbers recorded | This night was past the 80% mark you set. |

Read "past" as "on the far side of the mark in the direction you asked for". A booking window counts down, so a night 2 days out is past a 3-day mark, not short of it.

For a pickup rule, a room night counts as one, so a 3-room booking for one night reads as 3 here. [Pickup count](@37) has the detail.

A pickup rule with **Pickup measures** set to **Revenue (currency)** fires on the money booked, but its sentence still shows the room nights and calls your amount a booking mark. A rule set at 500 reads "9 bookings arrived in the last 3 days, past the 500-booking mark you set." The 500 is the amount you typed, in your property's currency, and the 9 is the room nights gained in those days.

The sentence opens with the level the rule is written for, then the count, then what a night like this usually has:

| Level in the rule | Opening words |
|---|---|
| Stalled | Bookings all but stopped this past week |
| Surging | Bookings surged this past week |
| Normal | Bookings came in at the normal pace this past week |
| Any other level | The level in lower case: "Bookings came in faster than normal", "Bookings came in much slower than normal", and so on |

"this past week" becomes "this past day" or "this past month" to match the rule's **Measured over** setting. A rule that cuts counts full days only, so its sentence reads "in the week up to yesterday" and "usually gets in those days". Then:

"Bookings came in faster than normal this past week: 9, against the 5 a night like this usually has by now."

The count can read "none" or, after cancellations, "more cancelled than booked". When similar nights usually have fewer than 1 booking by that point it reads "where a night like this usually has almost none by now".

**After the night has already been raised or cut.** Once a rule has changed a night, it counts only the bookings made since the newest change on that night by itself or by a stronger rule that moves the price the same way. The log cannot say which of those rules made the change, so the sentence names both and the days counted. For a raise, the day of the raise is the first day:

"Bookings came in much faster than normal in the 4 days since this rule or a stronger one's latest raise still on this night: 12, against the 5 a night like this usually gets in a whole week."

"in a whole week" is for a rule that raises on a fast pace: those bookings alone had to beat a whole window of a similar night. Any other rule reads "usually gets in those days". When only the day of the raise has been counted so far, it reads "later on the day of this rule or a stronger one's latest raise still on this night" and, for any other rule, "usually gets in a day". After a cut the count starts on the day after it, in full days: "in the 3 full days after this rule or a stronger one's latest cut still on this night". [How rules run](@39#counting-after-a-change) explains why the count restarts.
When an occupancy rule measured room types that do not count as rooms, those were left out of the figure, and one more sentence says so: "That 82% leaves out Meeting Room."

A booking speed or pickup rule can act on the same night again after its wait. The second time reads Then "Hot-week surge" raised it another 25%, from $206.25 to $257.81. The repeat only carries a "why" sentence when the run has fresh numbers for it.

**Example: Two rules and a ceiling on one night** · Deluxe on Friday, November 13, 2026 starts at $200. "Warm-date bump" raises it 10% to $220. "Hot-week surge" then raises it 25% to $275. The Deluxe ceiling is $400, so $275 is published. Had the ceiling been $250, the log would add: That would have gone past your $250.00 ceiling for Deluxe, so it stopped there.

A manual price shows as its own change, led by a sentence naming who typed it:

"Priya set the base rate to $180.00."

The name is the person's profile name in MAYA. If no name is stored it reads "A manager". A price our staff typed for you reads "MAYA support set the base rate to $180.00." A rate you changed in your property system on a night MAYA had sent to names no person: "The base rate was changed in Cloudbeds to $180.00." (or "in Think Reservations").

With nothing stacked on top, that one sentence is the whole entry, and the bold line reads "$180.00 up to $180.00 (+0%)". If a rule later fires on top of your price, its sentences follow the lead sentence in the usual way.

When you answer the **Rules that keep adjusting** banner, the answer is logged as its own item headed "Your answer · Fri, Oct 2, 2026, 3:12 PM PDT". One item covers every night the answer settled:

- Priya stopped "Hot-week surge" on 4 nights. What it already changed stays, unless cancellations mean the rule is no longer true.
- Priya stopped "Slow-date trim" on Fri, Nov 13 2026. What it already changed stays. (A rule with its undo box unticked.)
- Priya told "Hot-week surge" to carry on with 4 nights.
- Priya let "Hot-week surge" run again on 4 nights. It can start adjusting again from the next pricing run.

When our staff change something on your property for you, each save is logged as its own item headed "Changed by MAYA support · Fri, Oct 2, 2026, 3:12 PM PDT", with one line under it saying what changed:

- Changed by MAYA support: Took pricing live.
- Changed by MAYA support: Changed the pricing rule "Hot-week surge": action_value from 10 to 15.
- Changed by MAYA support: Changed the pricing rule "Hot-week surge": action_value from 10 to 15, 12 days.
- Changed by MAYA support: Removed a team member.

When you are live and a price cannot be delivered, the log carries an amber item headed "Prices not reaching Cloudbeds" (or "Think Reservations"). How soon it appears depends on the cause:

- **A problem that needs you**, such as lost access or a price your system refuses: at once.
A problem that needs you

- **Your system cannot find the rate MAYA writes to**: after one more try. MAYA reads your list of rates again and sends once more on the next run, about five minutes later. If the rate is still missing, the item appears then.
Your system cannot find the rate MAYA writes to

- **A problem that often clears on its own**, such as your system not answering, asking MAYA to slow down or not confirming a send: only once a night has failed at least 5 times over at least 2 hours.

A few holds MAYA applies itself never appear here.

While the problem lasts it sits at the very top, above every run. Once it ends it drops to where it ended, and only stays while that moment is within the runs shown. Mews never has these items, because nothing is sent to Mews.

The item names the cause in one sentence, counts the nights and room types affected, says "Still happening" or when it was resolved, and tells you what to do when there is something to do. **Show 12 tries** opens the attempts behind it. [When your property system does not accept a price](@57) walks through every cause.
A problem that often clears on its own

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Runs on screen | The 10 most recent that changed a price, however long ago. Quiet runs between them are counted into one line per stretch, shown under **Show All Cycles**. |
| Changes per run | The 40 biggest moves, largest first, each measured as the whole move from the night's starting point. A run with more changes shows its 40 biggest, then a line under them such as "And 23 more changes in this run." In a very large run, where more than about 1,000 nights ended at their starting point and not every one was checked for a move back, the count is a minimum and the line reads "And at least 23 more changes in this run." |
| What counts as a change | A night whose price differs from its starting point by at least one cent, has a rule still on it, or has a price someone set, and a night put back at its starting point. |
| Problems and answers | Up to 20 problems still happening, and up to 20 that have ended and 20 answers within the span of the runs shown. |
| Detail behind a change | Kept for 90 days. That is how long **Show the numbers** can open for a change. |

How far back 10 changes reach depends on your property: on a busy day perhaps an hour, on a quiet week several days. Older runs are not lost the moment they leave the screen, but there is no way to page back to them in the app.

The log lists nearly every price move:

- **A price going back to its starting point** is listed, from the price it had: the only rule on the night stops holding (for "Busy nights", the night falls to 80% full or less), cancellations take its only change off, or you clear a price you set on a night no rule is on. The entry names what came off and ends "That took this night from $165.00 to $150.00."
A price going back to its starting point

- **A price that moves only because its starting point moved**, on a night no rule is on, reads "The base rate for this night changed from $150.00 to $160.00." On Cloudbeds and ThinkReservations that includes a new rate MAYA reads from your system (about once an hour). On Mews, it is a newer booking with a different rate.

Two things are left out: moves past the 40 biggest of a run, which are only counted ("And 23 more changes in this run."), and a night arriving in the 396-night window at its starting point with nothing on it. To see where a night stands now, open the **Calendar** tab.
A price that moves only because its starting point moved

The log shows only the 10 most recent runs that changed a price. On a busy day a change from this morning may already have left it. MAYA keeps the detail behind every change for 90 days: the night's starting price and the price published, which rules acted, and the numbers each one saw. [Email us](mailto:info@modern-hospitality-solutions.com?subject=Why%20did%20a%20price%20change) with the room type, the night and roughly when the price moved, and we can look the change up for you within those 90 days. After 90 days the detail is gone.

There is no screen that shows one night's price history. The **Calendar** tab shows each night's current price, with a badge while a price typed in MAYA or changed in your system is in place. It does not show the prices the night had before. To keep your own record, copy the entries you care about while they are still in the log.

The sentences under each change follow your property's currency: "$" for US dollars, "€" for euros, "£" for pounds, and the three-letter code in front of the amount for any other currency. The calendar and the Rate Simulator use the same sign. The bold line above the sentences always shows "$", so a property in euros sees "€150.00" in a sentence and "$150.00" in the bold line for the same price.

Everyone on the property can read the change log, whatever their role.

An occupancy rule set to Greater than 80 writes: It was 85% full, past the 80% mark you set.

**Not yet** · The log cannot be exported, and MAYA does not email it or send notifications when a price changes. You cannot see more than the 10 most recent runs that changed a price, or page back through older ones. To keep a record, open the log and copy what you need.

Under a change in the change log, click **Show the numbers** to see the numbers behind it: how many bookings arrived for that night, how many a night like it usually has by then, and the level that reads as. It shows on a change when the run read booking speed for that night. **Which nights were compared?** shows how the similar nights were chosen, and which days of the week they fall on. **List the nights** lists them one by one, and each one can be set aside if it was not a normal night.

**Show the numbers** sits under a change in the change log, after its sentences. It appears under any change on a night where the run took a booking speed reading. A booking speed rule that measures the whole property (every booking speed starter rule does) reads each night it is not waiting on, and that reading goes under every room type's change on the night. So with such a rule on, nearly every change has the button, whichever rule made it: an occupancy, booking window or pickup rule, a price you typed, or a rate changed in your system. The evidence describes how the night was booking, not necessarily the rule that made this change.

The button is missing when the run took no booking speed reading for the night: you have no booking speed rule on, or each one was in its wait on that night. A rule that measures only some room types puts its reading only under the room types it changes.

To find the block behind a booking speed rule's change, read the first sentence of each. Usually it is the block for the rule's **Measured over** setting: "In the last 7 days" for a 7-day rule that raises, "In the 7 full days up to yesterday" for one that cuts. But a rule may find the night already raised within that stretch, by itself or a stronger rule, with that raise still on the price. Then it counts only the bookings since, and its block begins "The newest raise still on this night's price". A rule that cuts works the same way after a cut, with "The newest cut still on this night's price".

Say "Warm-date bump" raises a night on a Monday, and "Hot-week surge" raised it the Friday before. The surge changes the price by more, so it is the stronger rule, and the bump counts only the bookings since the surge's raise: its block starts "The newest raise still on this night's price" and covers those 4 days, not 30. The bump's raise never moves where the surge counts from. When the surge raises the night again within 7 days of its own raise, its block starts the same way. Two rules that count from the same raise over the same days show the same numbers, so two blocks can look alike.

If a change turns out to carry no reading, the panel says "No booking speed numbers were saved for this change." If the fetch fails you see the error and **Try again**. **Close** folds the panel away.

Three sentences, then sometimes a fourth.

**What arrived.** "In the last 7 days, 9 bookings arrived for this night, with 40 days still to go before arrival." The stretch matches the rule's **Measured over** setting. For a rule that cuts it counts full days only, ending yesterday: "In the 7 full days up to yesterday, 9 bookings arrived for this night, ...". When the rule measures some room types only, the count names them: "In the last 7 days, 9 Standard and Deluxe bookings arrived for this night, ...". A booking that holds several rooms counts once.
What arrived

**What is usual.** "By this point, nights like this one usually get about 5 bookings over the same stretch." When similar nights had fewer than 1 booking over that stretch it reads "almost no bookings". The number is what the similar nights had received over the same stretch of their own booking curves, at the same distance before arrival. It is their average, with the highest and lowest left off when there are 5 or more similar nights, and rounded to a whole number wherever it is shown.
What is usual
**The reading.** "That reads as Faster Than Normal." This is the level the count and the usual number produce together. [Booking speed](@34) has the seven levels and where the lines fall.
The reading

**A note when a fixed check moved the level.** Sometimes the numbers point one way and a fixed check keeps the reading nearer Normal. One of three notes then appears:

| Note | What happened |
|---|---|
| "The numbers leaned away from Normal, but by too little to matter at this many bookings, so it stays Normal." | The difference between the count and the usual number was too small to mean anything at that volume. |
| "The numbers pointed one step further from Normal, but not clearly enough, so it reads one step closer to Normal." | The count was high, but not by enough bookings to support the strongest level. |
| "Only a few similar nights were found, so it stays within one step of Normal however strong the numbers look." | Fewer than 5 of the similar nights had any bookings on record, so the reading is capped one step either side of Normal. |

**Example: The Harbour Inn, a Friday six weeks out**

Friday, November 13, 2026 received 9 bookings in the 30 days to Friday, October 2. The similar Fridays in MAYA's reading of the last three years had about 5 by the same point. The first layer reads:
A note when a fixed check moved the level

In the last 30 days, 9 bookings arrived for this night, with 42 days still to go before arrival.
By this point, nights like this one usually get about 5 bookings over the same stretch.
That reads as Faster Than Normal.

"Warm-date bump" measures over 30 days and fires at Faster Than Normal or above, so it raised Standard 10%. Blocks for the past week and the past day usually sit under this one too, read for "Hot-week surge" and "Sudden-spike catcher". Each has its own level.

A rule never counts the same bookings twice for the same change. Once a rule has raised a night, it counts only the bookings made since the newest raise still on that night's price by itself or a stronger rule. So does every weaker rule that raises. Cuts work the same way among the rules that cut. A weaker rule's change never moves where a stronger rule counts from, and a raise never moves where a cut counts from, or the other way round. Only booking speed and pickup rules move the count: an occupancy or booking window rule's change never does. The first sentence then names the stretch:

"The newest raise still on this night's price, by the rule behind this reading or a stronger rule, was made on Fri, Oct 2 2026. In the 4 days from that raise on, 3 bookings arrived for it, with 39 days still to go before arrival."

When the raise was earlier the same day, the second sentence reads "Later that day," instead: "... was made on Fri, Oct 2 2026. Later that day, 2 bookings arrived for it, with 42 days still to go before arrival." After a cut it reads "The newest cut still on this night's price", then "In the 3 full days after that, up to yesterday," since a rule that cuts counts whole days from the day after its cut.

The count starts again only when a price actually changes. A change that comes off because of cancellations no longer counts, so the rule goes back to counting from the change before it, or over its whole window. A change the cancellations leave on stays where it was, and counting still runs from when it was made.

A price you type on that night starts the count over: the rule waits its wait, in whole days from the day you typed, then reads its whole window again.

A night with no usable similar nights and nothing nearby to read from gets no reading at all, and no booking speed rule is allowed to act on it. The first layer then reads:

"There isn't enough booking history yet to say what is usual for this night."
"Booking speed wasn't rated for this night, so rules that watch booking speed left it alone."

You will see this on a change made by some other rule on a night whose booking speed was checked but could not be read.

Click **Which nights were compared?** and a short list appears under the first layer. Each line says how the similar nights were chosen. The lines are worked out from the nights themselves, so they always agree with the list under **List the nights**.

For a rule that cuts, the first line is "A rule that cuts counts full days only, up to yesterday, on this night and on the nights it is compared with alike."

- **The days of the week.** When every night compared is the night's own weekday: "Only other Friday nights were compared, since each night of the week books in its own way." When too few of those matched and other nights of the same kind were added, the line names them: "Too few other Friday nights matched, so Saturday nights were compared too, since they are also weekend nights. Friday and Saturday nights count as weekend nights, the rest as weekday nights." When none of the night's own weekday matched it says "were compared instead". A Wednesday can have Sunday, Monday, Tuesday or Thursday nights added, never a Friday or Saturday. Near a holiday the nights are lined up by the holiday, so their weekday can change from year to year:
The days of the week

- **The holiday or the season.** A night near a US holiday reads "This night is near Thanksgiving, so it is compared with the same days around Thanksgiving in earlier years, not the same date." Any other night reads "Only nights in the same season of your history were compared: Peak Season (June 10 through August 31)." When too few nights matched in the season and nights of the same weekday from around the same time of year were added, it reads "Nights in the same season of your history were compared: Peak Season (June 10 through August 31). Too few matched there, so nights within 45 days of the same time of year were added." When none came from the season, it says so and that those nights "were compared instead". Seasons are stretches of your year that book differently, read from your own history, and this line is the only place they appear on screen.
The holiday or the season

- **When the search was widened.** "Fewer than 4 nights matched closely, so the search was widened. Check the nights below and set aside any that were not normal." It means fewer than 4 nights matched on the strict rule (same weekday, same season), so MAYA allowed the same kind of night (a Saturday for a Friday, since both are weekend nights) or a nearby time of year. The lines above name what was added.
When the search was widened
- **Always last.** "Closed periods, and any nights you have set aside as not normal, are never compared."
Always last

A night with no similar nights at all is read from momentum instead: how nights near it are filling now, against how the same nights were filling a year ago. The list then opens with two lines that say exactly that ("Your history has no usable similar nights for this one, so the usual number comes from booking momentum instead." and "Momentum here means how nights near this one are filling now, compared with how the same nights were filling at this point last year."), and adds:

- "6 nearby nights could be paired with the same nights last year." (or "No nearby night could be paired with the same night last year, so there is no telling whether the pace has changed.")
- "Those nights are filling about 20% faster than they were a year ago." (or "slower", or "at about the same pace as a year ago" when within 5% either way)
[Which past nights your rules compare with](@36) describes momentum in full.

Once the second layer is open, and when there are nights to show, **List the nights** appears. Click it for one row per night. The nights nearest in time come first, up to 8. For an ordinary night that is usually the same weekday, week after week, from the same season: first any nights of that season that have already passed this year, then the same season last year, then earlier years if there is room.

Three rows from the list for The Harbour Inn's Friday, November 13, 2026:

| Row | Meaning |
|---|---|
| "Fri, Nov 14 2025" then "4 bookings in the same stretch" | That Friday had received 4 bookings over the same stretch, at the same distance before arrival. |
| "Fri, Nov 7 2025" then "1 booking in the same stretch" | The Friday a week before, read the same way. |
| "Fri, Oct 24 2025" then "6 bookings in the same stretch" | The next Friday back. Fri, Oct 31 2025 is not in the list: it is Halloween, and a night near a holiday is never compared with an ordinary night. |

A row can also read "no history for this night". MAYA has no bookings recorded for that night, usually because it falls before your history begins. It adds nothing to the usual number and does not count toward the 5 similar nights a full-strength reading needs.

Under each date, in smaller type, the reasons it was chosen, joined by semicolons: "a Friday; your Shoulder Season; about a year earlier". The season is your own, so its name on your screen can differ. When the match was loosened, the stricter matches are listed first, and a looser row can read "a Saturday, similar to a Friday; your Shoulder Season; about a year earlier" or "a Friday; a nearby time of year; 2 years earlier". The last reason says how long ago the night was: "earlier this year", "recently", "about a year earlier", "2 years earlier" or "3 years earlier".

For a momentum reading the rows are the paired nights, listed on their year-ago date: "3 bookings at this point last year, against 5 bookings now for Fri, Nov 6 2026", with the reason "used to read how the pace has changed since last year". The starting point night reads "4 bookings at this point last year, the starting point for the estimate", with the reason "this same night a year ago".

On the right of each row is **Not a fair comparison?**. Once you have set a night aside, that spot reads "Set aside. Not used from the next run on." [Setting a date aside](@49) walks through the form.

In this example The Harbour Inn's booking history only goes back to September 2025. The third layer lists 8 Saturdays, nearest first. Five have bookings on record, with 1, 4, 5, 5 and 6 bookings in the same stretch. The three oldest fall before the history begins and read "no history for this night", so they add nothing. The usual number is the average of the middle three of the five, about 5, because with five nights the highest and lowest are left off.

The 1-booking night is Sat, Nov 15 2025. Sam recalls the road closure that weekend and clicks **Not a fair comparison?** on it. From the next run that Saturday is left out, and an older Saturday moves up into the list. It too falls before the history begins, so it adds nothing. The usual number stays about 5: the 1-booking night was already left off as the lowest, and the four that remain average 5. But with only four similar Saturdays that have bookings, the reading can now go no further than Faster Than Normal, so "Hot-week surge" (which waits for Much Faster Than Normal) will not fire on this night while that holds.
